reviews.review_text: This hardly needs another 5 star rating, but I couldn't resist!  This was delicious!  I used a mix (about 50/50) of panko and italian seasoned breadcrumbs, and for the dressing I used a Parmesan ranch.  I cooked the chicken a little bit longer because it wasn't fully thawed.  I placed a cooling rack on a baking sheet, but the bottom still was a little bit soggy.  I'll find a way to fix that next time.  But it was such a tasty chicken dish!  Very moist chicken, good breading on the outside.  I was a bit worried about having uncooked chicken (most of my attempts at baking chicken without a precook in a pan don't go exactly as planned) but this was wonderful!  Next time I'll probably pound the chicken a little flatter so I don't brown the breading so much in an effort to cook it all the way through, and I'll probably add some shredded cheese the last couple of minutes.

attributes.source_text: Very moist chicken

reviews.review_text: I enjoyed this and my family enjoyed this. I have another ranch chicken recipe, but it takes 3 times as long to make and uses bone-in chicken, which some of my family members don't like. This one is not quite as good, but it is "good enough" and I can certainly see myself making this one far more often. The only problem I had was that I ran out of breadcrumbs. Next time I would double the breadcrumb mixture. I used 1/3 c. of cheese (cotijo instead of parmesan, but it is essentially the same) and 1 tsp. each of pepper and garlic powder. I actually had plenty of dressing. I cooked this on a rack in a half-sheet pan to try to make it more crispy. It still was not particularly crispy (maybe due to the lack of crumbs) so next time I might actually cook it straight on foil in the half-sheet to ease cleanup. I wouldn't use a smaller pan, though. I served this with Recipe #72735 and Recipe #321880.

attributes.source_text: my family enjoyed this

reviews.review_text: This is in my regular rotation - I can't believe I never reviewed it! I use Italian seasoned breadcrumbs. I'm a fan of "easy," so I put the chicken in the baking dish (with aluminum foil lining the bottom of course), spread some ranch on top, flip the breast over, pour a little more ranch on that side, and then shake the bread crumb mix over the top of it! I omit the butter as I don't think it needs it. My other handy hint: if you make it my way, then the chicken has never touched the bread crumbs, and you can throw the crumb/cheese mix in a Tupperware and put it back in the fridge for next time. Trust me, you'll be wanting to make this again! Side note: I made this with pork chops one night - TO DIE FOR!

This had a good flavor. I added 1 1/2 teaspoons dry Ranch seasoning mix to the crumb mixture, and I used a little more garlic powder than called for. I brushed the Ranch dressing on with a pastry brush, and I had just the right amount of crumb mixture. I didn't use butter; instead, I sprayed the pan and the chicken lightly with cooking spray. I baked them at 425 for 26 minutes, flipping once at half the time. My chicken didn't brown, but it cooked through fine and tasted good (I had mine on the middle rack - I didn't see the "setting rack to lowest position" thing until just now - lol). I served this with mac and cheese and steamed broccoli. I might do this again, next time with the oven rack set in the right place. ;) Thanks, I'm glad we tried it.

Kittencal...you've done it again!!!  Dang was this excellent!!!!!!!!  I used the panko bread crumbs and probably used 1/2 cup of fresh grated parmesan cheese for the coating.  I also added in some crushed red peppers and some Garli Garni (my favorite seasoning!).  I only had 1/2 cup of ranch dressing to my 3 extremely large chicken breasts and it was the perfect amount.  I followed another reviewers advise of baking the chicken on a rack on a foil lined baking sheet.  PERFECT!  Nothing soggy about my chicken tonight and my husband thought it was a home run!  I used margarine (all I had) and also was perfect.  We will definitely be making this one again and again.  Super quick, super easy!  Kitten...I'll be making MANY more of your recipes.  They never fail and are always sure to please.  Thank you!!!

reviews.review_text: I had to tweak this one because of ingredients on hand but the end result was terrific.  Moist, flavorful and crunchy.  What I thought was a new bottle of Kraft Ranch was actually Creamy Italian.  I slatherd 2, separated,  Leg-Quarters, Skin-On, in enough dressing to coat.  Let them marinate for 2 hours.  Sticking with the "Italian" theme I dredged the pieces in Italian breadcrumbs, Panko and freshly grated Parmegianno Reggiano then placed on a broiler pan to allow the drippings to fall through and baked at 375 for 1 hour.  Because I left the skin-on I omitted the butter and because I was worried about the salt content from the seasoned breadcrumbs and the fresh cheese I left out the salt.  The end result was a fabulous, flavorful, crunchy baked chicken, however, it did need the added salt.  This is a delicious chicken recipe and one I've already shared with my Dad who loves nothing more than a good chicken dinner.  Thank You!!

reviews.review_text: This came out really great. I omitted the seasoning salt and used salt and italian seasoning in its place to go with the oven roasted taters I was making. I preheated my baking stone (it has a rim) and put the chicken on it, topped the breasts with the leftover breadcrumbs, drizzled with the butter and baked for 20 minutes, then lo broiled for another 10 to crisp up the top. reviews.review_text: I had chicken breasts to prepare for dinner and made this. I'm not afraid to rate a recipe appropriately. But, from experience Kittencal has always come through with terrific recipe results. I used panko (1 cup) and because I was getting bold with this adventure I added 1/4 cup of canned italian bread crumbs to the dry mixture. In response to those who have a "soggy" problem I would question the bread crumbs you are using. In the past I used bread crumbs I grated from sandwich bread and in doing so my breading never ever produced a crispy crust. Just a note Panko is sold at the grocery store in the canned bread crumb section or in the oriental food section and works GREAT. Kitten, the big test is always my husband. He is picky. And, I have him trained to tell me his honest opinion about my cooking. He raved about this chicken. He just kept saying "man this is good." And, I agree the taste is spectacular. During baking I turned each chicken piece a few times. They got cripsy and very moist and tasty. One more note, I added spray butter and I'm sure it was because of the Panko that still made it end up crispy. Thanks for another 10 star keeper recipe Kitten! Man it was good!

reviews.review_text: Wow! I usually don't eat chicken breast, because I always dry it out and find it flavorless - but I had to buy some this week because it was on sale for only 1.99/lb, lol.. Needed to find something to do with it, and found your recipe, and I had every ingredient.. The reviews sold me - and I have to agree with them - I couldn't believe how flavorful and moist this chicken was! And crunchy on the outside! I was really surprised at how moist and juicy the ranch dressing makes the chicken, and once it's cooked, the ranch adds a little extra flavor without being at all overpowering. reviews.review_text: YUM!!! This was great! My family loved this. It's a keeper!!! Thanks, Kittencal for a really easy, yummy recipe. They took about 30 minutes and were perfect. I can't wait to try more of your recipes, Kittencal.

reviews.review_text: This transforms the ordinary and usually "boring" chicken breast into something to be craved at least once a week!  I halved the recipe just b/c there is only two of us... I didn't marinate the breasts in the ranch since I was a little short on time, but I will next time to see if it makes a difference. items.label: Crock Pot Lasagna
items.name: Crock Pot Lasagna
items.description: Make and share this Crock Pot Lasagna recipe from Food.com.
instructions: Brown ground beef, onion and garlic in frypan.
Add tomato sauce, tomato paste, salt and oregano.
Cook long enough to get it warm.
Spoon a layer of meat sauce onto the bottom of the slow cooker.
Add a double layer of uncooked lasagna noodles (break to fit) and top with cheeses.
Repeat with sauce, noodles and cheeses until all are used up.
Cover and cook on low for 4 to 5 hours.

reviews.review_text:
A testiment to the quality of this recipe:

I, the queen of bloopers, can honestly say this is a good recipe.  I thought I was being smart, I was making chili at the same time which has the same base ingrediants, so i'm happy as a clam, frying up hamburger garlic and onions.  I get the chili all made and simmering, go to assemble the lasagna and realize I loaned my big crockpot to a friend for Christmas.  ACK!  Improvise!  So I find my little corckpot (single person size I guess?, look at it for a moment then cheerfully decide, oh this will be fine i'll just cut back some things.  Okies, I'm gettin' into the grove here and put my layer of sauce in, go to the cupboard... and oh crud there's no lasagna noodles.. UGH.. Looking through I see a box of bow tie pasta, and in my mind compare the noodle thickness.  I say.. erm.. well nothing ventured nothing gained.  So I put just a bit more pasta in.. and realized I'd used basil... not oregano **slaps her forehead**... so I sprinkle a little on with each layer.  I didn't want cottage cheese (lactose) so really with that out I got a normal portion in for the full recipe.  9 hours on low in my teeny little crockpot.  It was really yummy, reminding me of baked ziti or rigatoni.  Thanks for the recipe Derf.  Signed.. The blooper queen of cooking.

I don't know what happened, but mine got burnt badly. I put everything in the crock pot in the morning, then put it in the fridge for my wife to turn on around noon. She turned it on high for an hour since it had been in the fridge, and then down to low. When I got home from work, the top of the lasagna already looked burnt.

I hesitate to blame the recipe completely for this, as the cooking time is only a guideline. Maybe my crock pot runs significantly higher than everyone else's. It would have been nice to have a warning. Most other recipes I've tried had significantly more liquid, which mitigated the ingredients drying out. This recipe is pretty "dry", and I even added 2/3 cup of water around the edge like others have mentioned.

I can't see this crock pot lasagna being significantly easier to fix than a regular lasagna. You can either boil the noodles for a few extra minutes, or use no-boil noodles. Simply assemble the lasagna in a 9x13 pan and bake covered until hot - which shouldn't take long. After all - one of the advantages of using a slow cooker is that you can leave it unattended; if this lasagna needs to be watched to keep it from burning, then there's really no point in doing it in a slow cooker.

Another problem is with the haphazard directions. Cook the meat, then dump it into a bowl, and only then add the onions separately. Garlic should be added after the onions are done sauteeing or it will burn. The tomato paste should also be cooked for a few minutes before adding the tomato sauce to eliminate the raw tomato flavor. You can then add the meat back in to finish the sauce.

I'll start off by saying that I've NEVER made a good lasagna.  This may be because of the intense hands-on time required for boiling noodles, layering, etc.  I have, however, tasted plenty of good lasagna (props to Stouffer's and, of course, Mom!).  I changed out several things, but this, bottom line, was awesome!  I did exchange the beef for ground pork and used dried garlic and onion then added 3 Tbsp brown sugar to the tomato mixture (used 1 oz tomato sauce more than written) to help cut some of the acidity (next time I may add a bit more as it was still a bit too acidic for my taste).  I also used 16 oz. cottage cheese and stirred-in 1/2 lb. cooked chopped spinach and 1 egg; in addition, I used 16 oz lasagna noodles.  Finally, I didn't have enough mozzarella on hand so I used 4 oz mozzarella, 8 oz cheddar, and an extra 4 oz of parmesan.  Still had a great flavor.  I had 3 nice layers, saving a bit of the cheese to put on top.  I think that even 4 hours may be a tad too long, though, but I can't tell for sure.  I ended-up cooking mine 4 hrs. 45 min (because I got doing other things and forgot the time) and a few edges were a bit tough.  Like other reviewers, I may use a bit of water around the edges next time (yes, there will be a next time).  Overall, though, I'd have to say AMAZING.  Thanks so much for making my (lasagna) dreams come true!!!

No messing around with pans of boiling water and draining pasta in a colander: fantastic!  This recipe is so much easier than stovetop/oven baked recipes.  A cinch to prepare, without any compromising of what lasagna-lovers expect of a good lasagna. Great winter dish, as well as being a wonderful way to make lasagna in the summer months.  I made only minor changes, to meet our taste preferences.  I doubled the garlic, added some thinly sliced mushrooms in step one, omitted the tomato paste (an ingredient I always omit), used MarraMamba's <ahref="/273976">The Simplest Tomato Sauce Ever (Marcella Hazan) 273976 which, since discovering it, has remained my favourite quick tomato sauce recipe.  I also added 1/2 cup of red wine in step two, and allowed it and the moisture from the mushrooms to reduce a little before adding the layers to the crock pot.  Thank you, Derf, for a wonderful recipe, discovered through the "I recommend... tag game".

I have never had much success with my crockpot recipes - they always turn out mushy, burnt, or flavorless. But when I saw all the 4-5 star reviews on this - I knew I had to try it! I followed the recipe exactly except I subbed the ground beef for a veggie beef. Then I started reading all the other reviews which had called for watering the pasta layers or pouring red wine over them or using the no-bake noodles and I got a little nervous that maybe I missed a step. I really didn't need to be - it came out fine in about 4 hrs using the recipe. It was a little crusty around the edges, but that's exactly how I like my lasagna. I cooked this in a Rival oblong crockpot so I'm sure the cooking time will depend on what size crockpot you use. I think it's important to note that this wouldn't be something that you would want to put together and then check it after a full work day (some reviews did this and claimed it was burnt) until you see how it works in your crockpot. I had to watch mine carefully because it only has 2 low settings - 8 and 10 hrs before it switches to warm, so that wouldn't have worked. This was good warmed up too. I may tweak the spices a little bit so suit my needs (a little too salty for me), but all in all this is a great easy recipe. In all honesty, I prefer my regular oven lasagna, but it's so time consuming that I don't get make it that often. This is a great alternative that was popular with the family too. I give the taste 3 stars (liked it) and the ease of the recipe 5 stars (outstanding), so I settled on 4 stars overall. Thank you Derf!

attributes.source_text: It was a little crusty around the edges, but that's exactly how I like my lasagna
was popular with the family too

reviews.review_text: Absolutely Delicious!! Wanted to make crock-pot lasagna for a potluck and found this recipe, and was excited to see all the great reviews.  Have never made lasagna and was nervous about using a crock-pot.  Was most nervous about using regular uncooked noodles and having them get soft, but another reviewer set my mind at ease, and I set out to make it.  After reading all the reviews, I ended up using many of the suggestions.  For the meat sauce, I used Italian seasoning, 7-Herb Tomato Pasta Sauce, some salt, some pepper along with the tomato paste, onion and garlic.  I also added a small amount of Italian seasoning to the cottage cheese as suggested.  I left out the oregano (because it was in the pasta sauce), and the Parmesan (did not feel I needed it, was not missed).  I used a 16oz box of noodles, which added nicely to the thickness of the lasagna.  After setting aside meat sauce for the bottom of the crock and the top layer, I took the suggestion of a reviewer and divided the rest of the meat sauce, the cheeses and the noodles into 3's for the layers, this worked out well for my 5-quart crock.  Finally, I sprayed the crock with vegetable spray to help against sticking, layered everything according to the recipe, topped it off with the meat sauce, and added 1/2 cup of water around the completed lasagna as suggested by another reviewer.  The lasagna cooked perfectly with no sticking or burning in only 3 hours on low, it reheated very well the next day, and the noodles came out perfect!  Was a big hit at the potluck, with only one little piece remainingJ.  Definitely will keep this recipe and make it over and over.  Thanks so much Derf J.

attributes.source_text: Wanted to make crock-pot lasagna for a potluck
added nicely to the thickness of the lasagna

reviews.review_text: Excellent recipe, even though I tweaked it to make it vegetarian. I don't usually do that since I do eat meat, but we had other meatballs on the side, so I just added mushrooms and baby spinach to the sauce. It was beautiful with the specs of green, and absolutely delicious. I used Hunt's sauce, since the ingredients are simple, and there is a good salt content. Since the noodles are dried and unsalted, I thought a saltier sauce would be great. I seasoned the cottage cheese with some salt, pepper and garlic powder (just a pinch) and added an egg. I needed the whole 16oz of cottage cheese, so it worked out well that it came in that size. I layered that with a sprinkle of the mozz and parm, and had a nice bit of that leftover for the top. I also sliced some heirloom tomatoes on the top, and cooked for the full 4hrs. It probably needed around 3.5, since some of the edges were very well done. I added about a cup of water and a little red wine before covering the dish to help with sticking. Everyone raved about this dish, and will be making it again this weekend.

This is a great lazy day recipe. Instead of the mozzarella and parmesan cheese I used a pre-shredded blend of mozzarella, parmesan and ementhal cheese. I used a 680ml can of tomato sauce and added 120ml water and the tomato paste. Proceeded as written. I should have waded through all the reviews and I would have avoided the pitfall of overcooking- the bottom and sides were burned after 4 1/2 hours. Luckily any burned flavour hadn't travelled through the entire dish so we enjoyed this. I did find it a bit salty and it could use some spicing up for my taste, but this is a good basic recipe and the kids liked it. Now that I've gone back and read all the reviews I will follow other's advise of adding 1/2 to 1 cup water, finish with the meat and cheese layer, as opposed to noodles and cheese so the top layer gets cooked properly, reduce the salt to 1/2 tsp., and try some spicy italian sausage in place of the beef. Thanks!

attributes.source_text: the kids liked it

reviews.review_text: This was the first time I've ever made lasagna, and I'm so glad I waited until I found this recipe. Subs I made were: ground turkey for beef, whole grain noodles for regular, 2 lb container of fat free cottage cheese instead of 16 oz, fat free cheddar instead of mozarella and I added 1/8 tsp of Stevia to the sauce. I also only single layered the noodles. The lasagna turned out so well. I'm not sure why people needed to add water-mine had plenty of liquid, so I'm glad I didn't follow that suggestion. This a great way to get dairy and a tomato based item into my older son (he can't drink straight milk and hates tomatoes). My younger son (3 1/2) and husband had seconds. For our family, this made 10 huge servings with plenty left to freeze. Next time I plan to add mushrooms in the layers or with the sauce. The only other change I'll make the next time is to turn off the pot at 5 hrs-tonight I'd turned it to warm, and it got the noodles too soft. Still tasty though! Thanks for posting a fantastic recipe!

attributes.source_text: My younger son (3 1/2) and husband had seconds
My younger son (3 1/2) and husband had seconds

reviews.review_text: I was definitely nervous about lasagna in a crock pot, even after all the great reviews, but I must say, there was nothing to be worried about!  It took about 4 hrs on low in my crock pot. I made a few changes like sauteing spinach, chopped jalapeno pepper, and mushrooms along with the beef, onion, and garlic.  I used 1 can of stewed tomatoes and 1 can of  regular  sauce to make the 28 oz can of sauce, just because I like stewed tomatoes in my lasagna. I was about to  buy the no-boil lasagna noodles because I was nervous about using regular noodles, but decided to go with the regular noodles and it worked out fine.  Also, used ricotta instead of cottage cheese.  Lastly, I did not double layer the noodles, I just used one layer, which seemed to get lost with meat and cheeses.  Next time will use double layers like the recipe states. Great recipe for the crock pot!

This turned out yummy. I did 1lb ground beef and 1lb of Italian Sausage. I mixed that with 2 1/2 (had 1/2 jar in fridge) of Barilla's traditional sauce. I cooked the meat last night, but literally threw this thing together this morning. I used an entire 32 oz of ricotta...kind of spooned it on top of the noodles...flattened it out a bit, but wasn't at all going for TLC in assembly. I did use pam on the sides of my crockpot and also put in 1 1/2 cups of water around the edges. I set it for 5 hours on low and then it switched to warm. It likely stopped cooking around 1:30 and it was perfect when we cut into it at 6:00. It was warm on the outsides and still hot in the middle. It set up so well and cut like a really deep lasagna I'd bake. My kids loved it...and I'm thrilled because I get tired just thinking about making a traditional lasagna.

attributes.source_text: My kids loved it

reviews.review_text: I thought I'd add my rave reviews to all the others.  Who ever thought that lasagna could be so easy?  I did use about 1 1/2 cups more water than called for, added some Italian seasoning, about twice as much garlic and I also used lots of cheese.  I cooked it for 6 hours, but found that it was done before my bread machine was ready so I turned my crock pot down to warm for the last hour.  Even then it burned a bit on the bottom. (I'm glad I had sprayed the pot with Pam before using!)  The middle and top were delicious and I think that next time I'll cook it for less time.  I served it with #63380 Bread Machine French Bread Italian Style and a salad with my Peanut Butter Salad Dressing #98640.  For dessert we had #100032 Penelope's Lemon Peppyseed Cake.  My DH thought he had died and gone to heaven!  Thanks Derf for a great new recipe.

attributes.source_text: My DH thought he had died and gone to heaven!

reviews.review_text: Very good and easy.  Time intensive in gathering ingredients and putting it into pot, but after that it's easy cause the crockpot does the rest.  Warning: DO NOT ADD THE RECOMMENDED SALT: I would say do NOT add any salt at all cause tomato sauce and paste has salt in it (look at the can ingredients)--was Way too salty that way and I had to water it down.  You can always add salt later.  Taste the sauce before you put into crockpot. I did add about 1 T sugar. Next time  I will add fresh basil, and 1 more clove of garlic. But w/o those additions, it still had a nice mild flavor that I liked.  The cottage cheese 2 % tasted very good with this dish.  I cooked on high for 1 hour and low for 2 1/2 hrs, then lifted the lid to check on it, then kept it on low for another 1/2 hour.  A small portion of the bottom was slightly burnt but still OK (since portions of lasagne with the cheese are supposed to get slightly yellowed/burnt anyway).

attributes.source_text: it still had a nice mild flavor that I liked

reviews.review_text: This is so good! Just like many others have suggested, I used sausage instead of beef. I also like a meatier lasagna so I doubled the meat, used 1 1/2 onions and 4 cloves of garlic. I used one can of tomatoe sauce, a can of paste and a jar of pasta sauce. I added both Italian seasoning and basil. I picked up some amazing cheeses (ricotta, fresh motz and grated some parm) and layered them in with some mushrooms and spinach. It was a HUGE lasagna. It didn't spoon out very pretty but tasted amazing! I cook for my grandmother weekly and this has become a staple! It's easy and incredibly versatile. I suggest doing what your family likes and using these steps as your baseline. I also followed another posters suggestion of spraying the pot and adding a bit of water around the edges. It is always amazing!

Disclaimer: I am not a cook. This recipe was fantastic. I followed the directions pretty carefully. The dish turned out better than I could have imagined. I have a 6 quart slow cooker so that's the size I used. I upped the meat a little to make it heartier. I cut the salt down to 1 teaspoon (next time I might just leave it out all together). I used ricotta (the 15 oz size) instead of cottage cheese. I did spoon a large amount of the sauce mixture in the bottom based on other comments. I ran a little low on sauce on the top layer. I did pour half a cup of red wine along the sides. Oh, and before I started, I rubbed the inside of the slow cooker with olive oil. Cleanup was super easy. My flat mate and I both loved the dinner. I will definitely make this again and I highly recommend it to anyone - especially to other novices like me.

attributes.source_text: My flat mate and I both loved the dinner
both loved the dinner

reviews.review_text: I was so excited to see a good crockpot lasagna recipe with so many great ratings that I just had to try it!  I omitted the salt, used a 28oz can of diced tomatoes instead of the tomato sauce, then added a 6oz can of tomato sauce.  Used part skim ricotta instead of cottage cheese, and used a 12oz package of Morningstar Crumbles instead of ground beef, so my vegetarian husband could enjoy lasagna again.  I also added fresh spinach leaves to each layer. I ended up with 3 layers that fit perfectly in my crockpot.  I added a cup of water, but it was too watery (I had to spoon a lot out), so I think I won't add much water next time. I think it was because I used extra tomato sauce.  It was ready after 3 hours.  A big hit here in my house.  I'll be making it again!  Thank you so much Derf!

reviews.review_text: This was simple and delicious for a quick dinner. We are in the process of tearing up our kitchen for some remodeling and we were looking for an easy and quick dinner. We decided to try this and it turned out well. My stove is already out of the kitchen, but I have a rice cooker that also sautes, so I was able to brown the hamburger, onions, and garlic in the rice cooker and then let the sauce simmer for a few while I picked up my daughter from preschool. I assembled everything in the crockpot when I got home and ended up added about a cup and a half of water after it cooked for a while when I noticed the noodles tasted doughy. The water definitely helped with cooking the noodles and helped everything turn out delicious. Will definitely make it again for a quick dinner.

attributes.source_text: for a quick dinner
for a quick dinner

reviews.review_text: This was extremely easy and delicious!!  After reading all the reviews I made a few modifications and it turned out perfect!! When I browned the beef I added onion and let them brown together until the onion was almost soft then I added the garlic. I didn't have whole garlic I had minced in the jar so I added 2 TBL. I really like garlic though. While the garlic was cooking into the beef and onion I added oregano, basil, and Italian seasoning. I cut out the salt. I think that plain tomato sauce and paste is bland so I used a 24oz jar of Ragu, any flavor, and 14oz can of Italian flavored diced tomatoes. I followed the rest of the directions and it was moist, noodles were perfect and sooo flavorful!!!!  It was just like Grandma used to make only so much easier!!!

My DH loves lasagna and I almost never make it - with a newborn and a toddler in the house it just seems like too massive an endeavor! This recipe, however, was easy and AWESOME.

I left out onion because I detest it but otherwise followed ingredients exactly. This tastes like my mom's lasagna recipe (which I love). items.label: Perfect Pork Tenderloin
items.name: Perfect Pork Tenderloin
keywords: c("Meat", "Very Low Carbs", "High Protein", "Healthy", "High In...", "Potluck", "< 15 Mins", "Oven", "Beginner Cook", "Easy")
items.description:
My #1 way to cook a pork tenderloin or a boneless pork loin because it's ALWAYS moist and tender.  It's easy and foolproof!  If you like, marinate the roast and rub with any seasonings that please your palate! 

So many people have asked me how long to cook tenderloins if they have "more than one" to cook, I wanted to give a simple response.  ANSWER:  So long as the tenderloins are NOT touching each other, cook 3 or 4 individual tenderloins for the same amount of time as if you were cooking one.  Remember, each tenderloin is cooking in its own separate space.  EXAMPLE:  If cooking three 1-pound tenderloins, cook them only 5-1/5 minutes TOTAL.   This makes it a great entree recipe when having a dinner party for 8-12 people, or more.

If you enjoy this pork recipe and cooking method, you might want to try my similar beef cooking method - Recipe #65987.
instructions: NOTE:  The success of this cooking method will depend upon how accurate the temperature of your oven is and how well your oven retains heat.  Adjust cooking time +/- according to your individual oven.
NOTICE: If you have a very old oven that is not well insulated, this recipe may not work for you, as heat retention/residual heat is important to the success of this recipe.
Determine the EXACT weight of roast from the meat wrapper.  Weight will determine how long to cook the roast.
Preheat oven to 500 degrees.  Remove tenderloin from refrigerator.  Season meat as desired.  Place seasoned meat in an uncovered roasting pan on a shelf in the bottom 1/3 of your oven.
Bake EXACTLY 5 1/2 minutes PER POUND.  Adjust +/- according to your oven's accuracy and heat retention. NOTE:

IF YOU HAVE AN OVEN PROBE OR THERMOMETER THAT HAS A WIRE THAT GOES THROUGH THE SIDE OF THE OVEN DOOR, BY ALL MEANS USE IT AND SET THE TEMPERATURE ALARM FOR 140 DEGREES.  REMOVE MEAT FROM OVEN WHEN ALARM ALERT GOES OFF (probably before an hour has expired).

Turn oven OFF and DO NOT open oven door for 45 to 1 hour, OR sooner IF you are using a probe thermometer and it alerts that internal meat temp is at 140 degrees.  Remove pork from oven, lightly cover with foil, and let rest 5-10 minutes to redistribute internal juices.  Roast should be done, very slightly pink in the center, and very moist.
After resting 10 minutes, the roast should reach a safe 145-150 degrees.

NOTE:******* For anyone questioning this method of cooking, it really does reach the proper internal temperature on a thermometer.  According to Sara Moulton on FoodTV, trichinosos is killed at 138 degrees, and 145 is a safe temperature for pork, although the USDA recommends 160 degrees (meat will be much drier).  If the center of the meat is not a little pink, it is overcooked!

VARIATION:  To make Roasted Veggies along with the tenderloin, peel carrots and potatoes, and cut into about 1-inch cubes.   Season as desired and drizzle with a little oil.  Add vegetables to pan around (but NOT touching) pork tenderloin.  Cook tenderloin as instructed above.  The roasted potatoes and carrots should be done when the roast is done.  You may need to adjust the size of the potatoes and carrots depending upon the weight of your tenderloin and how long you cook it.

reviews.review_text: I have benefitted so much from this site and others like it I feel that I feel that it is time that I begin giving back by sharing my experiences. <br/><br/>I usually smoke pork loins on the Egg, but I saw this recipe and thought I'd give it a try. BeachGirl is correct; if you have a corded meat thermometer that will allow you to monitor the internal temperature of your loin while it cooks, by all means use it! Otherwise you are at the mercy of your knowledge of the insulating quality of your oven. Here's why I know that. <br/><br/>I cooked my 1.2 pound pork loin for exactly 6 minutes at 500 degrees, then turned off the gas and set the kitchen timer for one hour. I had inserted the temperature probe into the meat and programmed the thermometer to alarm when the meat reached an internal temperature of 140 degrees. In a mere 15 minutes, the thermometer was signaling 140 degrees. Skeptical, I rummaged around in that junk drawer we all have in the kitchen and found my instant read thermometer to double check the temp. Sure enough, it read 140 and rising. I tented the loin with aluminum, waited 10 minutes, and checked the temp again with both thermometers. To my surprise, the temp had climbed to 150, so I sliced the pork loin and tasted it. It was perfect. <br/><br/>I have a Viking brand stove and it must be almost airtight to have continued cooking the pork loin for a mere 15 minutes to reach 140 degrees. If I had left the meat in for the full hour I would have had pork jerky! Invest in a corded meat thermometer, it's worth it and costs less than one ruined beef tenderloin. Mine is a Polder and has a remote beeper that I can wear on my belt or sit on the kitchen counter while my meat is outside on the smoker, and that's great in the winter. <br/><br/>Oh, I rubbed the pork with olive oil then rubbed in fresh rosemary, fresh thyme, fresh chopped garlic, fresh ground pepper, and a little salt. Delicious, and perfectly done (medium to medium rare).<br/><br/>Thanks for sharing this, BeachGirl. I have long been a fan of cooking meat hot and fast to sear in the juice, and this recipe encourages me to continue!

FABULOUS! Not sure why I had such a hard time wrapping my head around cooking time calculations. Maybe it was that second cup of coffee that switched the light on for me. We are working in 5ths. (Note, 1 lb (base of 100)/5 min = 20 sec). So per the commentator below who was cooking a pork tenderloin weighing 1.54 lbs and calculating cooking time at 8.5 min This calculation does not take into account the other .5 lb per minute - why you were worried when your resting temp continued to rise to the temp it did - although by your account it turned out beautifully/not pink but juicy? Maybe this is the difference between medium/medium rare. (I don't know.) I'm printing this recipe off and also including it in my kids' recipe books I'm creating for them, along with "how to calculate the cooking time for pork *tenderloin*". They are new to cooking so, "following the man in the yellow jacket" is paramount to their success! This is an easy and excellent, no fail recipe for every skill level. Hoping others will find the following calculation examples helpful: Calculation for a 1.54 lbs tenderloin: 1 lb = 5 min 20 sec .5 lb = 2 min 40 sec (2 min 30 sec + 10 sec) .04 = 12 sec (60 sec x .04 = 2.4 sec x 5 min = 12 sec) Total cooking time 8 min 12 sec Here is a 2.3 lb tenderloin calculation: 1 lb = 5 min 20 sec 1 lb = 5 min 20 sec .3 lb = 1 min 30 sec (60 sec x .3 = 18 sec x 5 min = 90 sec; or, 1 min 30 sec) 20 sec+ 20 sec + 30 sec = 70 sec (carry 60 sec/l minute leaving 10 sec) 5+5+1+1 min carryover = 12 minutes Total cooking time 12 min 10 sec

I read almost every single comment on here before attempting to make this last night. I could see the potential of this being incredible, but I had some issues with my meat thermometer, and it turned out a bit drier than I would have liked. Still, it was very juicy and tender, despite being closer to well done. I bought a 1.2 pound pork tenderloin, dried it off with a paper towel, removed some of the fatty parts with a paring knife, rubbed in salt, pepper, garlic salt, and then placed it in a ziploc bag of a marinade using whole grain mustard, brown sugar, maple syrup, and minced garlic. I only let it marinate for a couple hours. I brought the meat out about an hour before I put it in the oven to bring it to room temperature. My oven is fairly new, but it took almost 40 minutes to preheat to 500 degrees. I had cut up baby potatoes and Brussels sprouts, tossed them in olive oil, garlic powder, herb de provence, salt and pepper, but made the mistake of putting them on a baking tray and putting the tray in the oven on the top shelf during the pre-heat phase when it was at 460 (I had read a comment about how the veggies took longer to cook and to put them in earlier). By the time the oven was pre heated to 500 degrees, the potatoes and Brussels Sprouts were already very crispy/borderline burnt. I let them rest on the stove during the meat cooking process, and popped them back in while the meat was resting. I had purchased a meat probe with a digital timer that stays outside the oven. Once I put the meat in, I timed it for about 6 minutes, then turned the oven off, and set my meat probe to alert me when it reached 140 degrees. 15 minutes later, my timer went off, saying the meat had reached 140 degrees (which seemed way too soon). So, I left it in the oven for 45 minutes, removed the meat, and used a different meat thermometer. It read 120 degrees (my meat probe was reading 190 degrees, so I think both were faulty). I tented it with tinfoil, let it rest for 10 minutes, and it still read 120 degrees. When I cut it, it was well done, and like I said, still pretty moist, considering. I definitely want to try this again, but next time I'll know not to trust my meat thermometers, and be more specific with using the time as an indicator.

reviews.review_text: This was an excellent recipe, very easy and delicious. I had to tweak the recipe somewhat because I used a toaster oven which only goes up to 450 degrees and I like my pork tenderloin cooked longer (medium well). While this may not be the most accurate review, it was what I could work with and shows the flexibility of the recipe. The first time I made this, I seasoned the (1.5 lb) pork tenderloin with just salt and pepper and baked at 450 degrees for 6.5 min./lb, turned the oven off and let it sit for 1 hr. It was 105 degrees afterwards and had virtually no color on the outside, so I broiled it, rotating once, for 15-20 minutes until the internal temperature was 155 degrees, which while drier, was perfect for me. I've since perfected the method to suit my tastes. I preheated the oven to 450 degrees (or set it to "broil"), pan-seared the outside of the tenderloin on all sides first (for color and additional heat), put it in oven, turned the oven off and let it sit for 45 mins. to an hour, depending on who I'm serving it to (internal temp 145 degrees to 155). On the rare occasion it doesn't come up to temp, I put it under the broiler for 10+ mins until internal temp is met. I've made it with different marinades and rubs and they have all been fantastic under this method. Thank you for sharing.

Perfect Indeed in Toaster Oven!!!! I have not seen a review for doing the Perfect Tenderloin in a Countertop Oven so here it is. It is sizzling here in Texas Summer so I moved my NuWave and Elite Countertop Rotisserie Ovens to garage, just off my kitchen, to keep heat down in apartment (and have more kitchen counter space). In addition the apartment stove/oven has questionable ability to retain heat or keep heat constant. (I hate this stove/oven. - We recently moved from big house with wonderful appliances.)... I brought 1.5 Tenderloin up to "room temp" by leaving it out of fridge for 1 hour. Then rubbed with seasonings/sea salt/ fresh minced garlic/butter rub and massaged in. I cut 4 slits in top and put some of the rub into slits. (Caution - We love our garlic but, with this manner of cooking, next time I'm going to lower the amount of garlic as it seemed to infuse more than I'm used to.) My "toaster" oven only goes up to 450 degrees F so I adjusted the amount of time for initial cooking of 5.5 minutes/lb due to lower initial cooking temp. After placing tenderloin on rack in small, shallow pan and folding skinny end under, so that both ends were as thick as middle of t-loin, and it made the t-loin fit the rack, I put it into preheated, to 450 F, for 12 minutes. As I was pretty sure the oven would not retain high enough heat for an hour, for the oven-off time, I set oven to "keep warm", about 150-160 F, for one hour. (Oven is NOT a convection, only upper and bottom coils for baking; no air circulation.) Soon after oven turned off I placed a meat thermometer into meat. It read 150-155 F. I let the t-loin rest in oven for an hour as I was busy with other cooking. It came out PERFECT; perfect pink interior. Never have I had a more perfectly moist, perfectly cooked pork tenderloin, either out at great restaurants or prepared in-home!!!! I'm sharing this with friend and I'm so looking forward to preparing other cuts of meat in this manner. Thank you, thank you for sharing this amazing way to cook Perfect Pork Tenderloin.

attributes.source_text: more perfectly moist

reviews.review_text: First, I’m a vegetarian so I have no idea how to cook meat but I was hosting Christmas dinner this year and wanted to accommodate all palates. I bought my pork tenderloins from Costco so there were two pieces of meat in each package but I froze one package and cooked the 2 pieces of meat in the 2nd package. I also bought a probe thermometer from Bed, Bath & Beyond just so I’d get an exact temperature reading. I read all the reviews. At least one of the reviews gave instructions about cooking 2 tenderloins at one time and that’s what I used for reference. I made sure to trim the silver skin off each tenderloin (I read somewhere else that you should trim the silver skin from the tenderloin), covered them with a dry brine, and placed both tenderloins in a glass Pyrex baking dish, making sure they did not touch. Before placing in the dish, I measured the larger tenderloin on a food scale and it was 1.54 pounds so I used that weight for the total cooking time. I followed the recipe exactly. I preheated the oven to 500 degrees, placed the tenderloins (with the probe thermometer in the larger piece) in the oven for 8.5 minutes then turned the oven off. I was so skeptical and nervous because when I turned the oven off, the meat temperature was only at about 85 degrees. But after about 30 minutes, the meat reached 140 degrees. I waited til it got to 143 degrees and removed them from the oven. I did not cover the tenderloins with foil at that point. I watched and watched as the temperature continued to rise while the meat was resting. At its highest, it got to 160 degrees and I was distraught thinking that I screwed it all up and it would be overcooked and dry. But when we finally sliced the tenderloins, they were absolutely perfect according to the meat eaters. My guests literally could not believe how perfectly cooked the tenderloins were and I could not have been happier. It kinda made me wish that I was a meat eater...! THANK YOU BeachGirl! You rock, sister! I will never cook tenderloins any other way.

reviews.review_text: It works! Like others, I had what I thought was one pork tenderloin but when I opened it, it was two pieces about equal in size. The total weight was 1.98 lb so I divided that in half to figure out how long to cook them. The day before I cooked them, I rubbed them with olive oil, fresh garlic, brown sugar, salt and pepper. I then marinated them in a ziploc bag overnight in a soy sauce, mustard, honey concoction (just used what I had lying around). Like the tip says, I made sure the two pieces weren't touching each other and cooked them as if they were separate, so 5 and a half minutes at 500 degrees, then turned the oven off, and didn't touch a thing. I took it out after about 48 minutes and my meat thermometer read about 158 right away. Let them sit for 10 minutes, sliced them up and they were perfectly slightly pink in the middle, so tender!! I also cut up potatoes and cooked those in a separate pan right in the oven with the pork. So easy! The potatoes were slightly underdone at the end so while the pork rested for the 10 minutes, I put some cheese on top of the potatoes and broiled them on high. They were perfect after that. Such an easy meal and so tasty. I'm planning on using the leftover pork with some ramen noodles tonight.

reviews.review_text: I had an 11 pound pork loin and couldn't find a single review from anyone who used this recipe with such a large cut, so I was quite nervous. My oven is also pretty old and I don't have an oven thermometer to check how accurate the thermostat is. I brined the meat for 6-8 hours before cooking using a salt and brown sugar brine. I forgot to take it out of the fridge to warm to room temp, so I was very nervous it was going to be late. I intended to bake it for the specified time but somehow accidentally reset my timer. I had to guess how much time to reset it for and guessed on the long side because I was so afraid it wouldn't cook in time. Anyway, by the time I had let it sit for about 45 minutes with the oven off, per the recipe, the meat temp was way higher than it should have been (I took the thermometer out when it reached 165 because I couldn't bear to see how much it had been overcooked.) Amazingly enough, everyone still loved it, including my father-in-law who is pretty much a meat expert and generally does not like meat well done! I thought it was a tad dry but not bad considering how much I overcooked it...and it was super tender. So I'll definitely be using this recipe again, and be watching my timer much more carefully!

reviews.review_text: For whatever reason, this did not work for me as written. I had a 5.54# pork loin and I followed the instructions, removing the meat after 45 minutes. I tented it with foil and rested it for 10 minutes and it temped at 133 degrees. I put it back in the oven at 500 for 10 minutes, retented & rested for another 10 minutes and it temped at 138. I put it back inside the oven (off but still very warm) for another 20 minutes, tent on because by now my wife and I had eaten all of the side dishes and I just wanted it to be over. I rested it for another 10 minutes and it finally temped out just a hair over 145. It could be that it really wanted an hour (instructions gave a 15 minute window of 45min to an hour) or that my oven is imprecise, though I've been in this apartment for 4 years and never had an issue unless I put something on the wrong rack, but this thing was needy. Turned out pretty well, but took a lot longer than I'd planned for and I had to postpone an outing to accommodate.

I had a Costco Pork Sirloin Tip Roast (part of the 4-pack they're selling these days) and tried this recipe with that cut of meat and it worked perfectly. We had made one of the other pork roasts a couple of weeks ago following the basic instructions on the package and it was dry. This time, I used the method described above and it was amazingly moist! So, YES, use this exact same method for more than just tenderloin!
A couple of things to note: bring your meat to room temperature before roasting (I always do this for any meat, and just wanted to bring that to the attention of those who may not know that trick). I rubbed the meat with a mixture of garlic, rosemary, celery salt, salt, pepper and oil. My roast was just under 2 pounds and I cooked for 10 minutes at 500 degrees, convection method. When I turned off the oven, I checked the actual oven temperature 50 minutes after turning it off and it was at 277 degrees. My oven is fairly high-end and I assume well-insulated so I'm thinking that if you have an old or poorly insulated oven that loses heat too quickly, it may work to set your oven at 250 or so instead of turning it off altogether. That way, it won't go below that point.

reviews.review_text: I will not rate this at this time. I have the bottom oven rack of my oven covered in quarry tiles for when I bake bread. These must have caused a 'more insulated' oven than most ovens.I put a 1lb pork tenderloin in for 5 minutes and turned the oven off. After 30 minutes it started to smell like it was really done....  and it was. It was overcooked. Next time I'll remove the baking tiles.<br/>UPDATE: I have done this 2 more times with great results. I removed the quarry tiles from my oven. While the pork doesn't look like it's done, this cooking method works well. I cooked the 1lb 3 ounce tenderloin for 6 minutes and left it in the oven for 40. An instant read thermometer says it's done. I season the pork the day before with black pepper.. adobo and rosemary and wrap it in plastic wrap. reviews.review_text: By FAR the definitive way to cook tenderloin... Yes, I know, it sounds odd to cook it with no heat for the vast majority of the cooking time, but trust me, it works like a charm, and not once have I had it come up a different temperature or finish than it should be, at the right time.  In fact, perfect example... I was just visiting a very close friend out in Colorado... She had a nice tenderloin she was planning on for dinner that night, and I said, "Ummm, let me direct you in cooking this, okay?"  She agreed, until she heard what I was planning, then all, well, "stuff" broke loose.  She is an amazing girl, but very careful in her cooking, and paranoid as the dickens when it comes to additives to food, how food is prepared, etc.  Finally talked her into it, and off we went.  She literally sat in front of the oven door window for the entire cooking time, twitching, while it cooked.  It got done, came out, sat for a wee bit as it should, then once the Quinoa and salad were done, we carved it up.  She was floored.  Tasting it was scary to her as well, but she did (love her for that!), and loved it.  She and her husband ate the left overs the next day... THAT was definitive proof that this recipe is a) the best, and b) works.  I season mine with garlic, rosemary, and onion...

UHHHHHH-MAZING! I have never been a fan of pork tenderloin, probably because I've only had the pre-seasoned kind. There are certain preservatives in the seasoned pork that I can actually taste, gross right? So I went on an adventure and bought a plain piece of pork tenderloin for $2.5, which was $4 cheaper than the same sized pre-seasoned pack.
I mixed garlic-rosemary-thyme-salt-pepper-butter into a paste which I placed into slits I cut all over the meat. I slathered the pork with the remaining paste. I placed the tenderloin on a roasting rack, put a little chicken stock into the roasting pan, and cooked it according to the recipe. It cooked up perfectly! I added the leftover baking liquids to some mushrooms I had sauteed, and threw in a bit of flour, which made an amazing mushroom gravy to the already delicious pork tenderloin.

Make this. You will not regret it!

I was a little leery at first because fear of undercooked pork is right up there with snakes and public speaking.  I cooked four tenderloins weighing a total of 5.5 lbs, making my "oven on" time (at 500, the highest my oven goes) calculate to 30 minutes.  I took an added "safety" measure by turning the oven back on at 350 for five minutes at ten minutes into "oven off" time, then turned the oven back off and let it cool naturally.  As recommended, I never opened the oven door to release any heat.  I took out the meat at the appointed time and added some water to the pan as the standing juice had all evaporated, leaving a brown residue.  The water and residue made a tasty au jus after I heated it in the pan and scraped the bottom.  Not that the roast need it.  As promised, the meat was fully cooked, moist and tender.  Excellent!

reviews.review_text: This is the BEST and only way to cook pork tenderloin!  I had a 1 1/2 pound pork tenderloin.  Prior to cooking I used salt, pepper and granulated garlic as a rub.  Placed the pork in a 9 x 13 pyrex glass dish and poured coke to cover about half of the loin.  I refrigerated it for 6 hours and removed it from the fridge about an hour before cooking to allow it get to room temperature.  As a glaze I mixed mustard, honey, brown sugar and cracked pepper in a bowl and poured it over the loin before placing it in the oven. I cooked it at 550 degrees for 9 min, turned off the oven and 1 hour later it was cooked to perfection! The meat thermometer read 160 (I believe) after it rested. I did leave some of the coke on the bottom of them pan hoping to use the sauce for the pork but it did burn slightly.  Next time I will try it without liquid on the bottom. Hands down the best way to cook pork tenderloin!  Thank you for sharing your great cooking technique!

instructions: In a mixer bowl, cream together sugar and butter; beat in egg and vanilla.
Combine flour, cinnamon, baking powder and salt.
Add to butter mixture.
Blend well.
Cover and refrigerate 2 hours or till firm enough to roll into balls.
Shape dough into small balls about 3/4-inch in diameter.
Roll in cinnamon sugar to coat.
Set cookies 1-inch apart on lightly greased cookie sheets.
Bake at 350° for 10 minutes or till the edges are lightly browned.
Cool slightly on pans, then remove to racks to cool completely.

reviews.review_text: I have enjoyed being creative with this delicious recipe.  Based on other reviews I used 3/4 cup of sugar and unsalted butter as well as a teaspoon measure for the cookie dough. The first time, I followed the recipe as written.  The second time I used 1/2 tsp EACH cinnamon, allspice, and pumpkin pie spice.  I divided the dough in half.  One half stayed "basic".  To the other half I added 1 1/2 tsp strong coffee and 1 T Kahluah (before chilling)After rolling the dough into balls, I flattened with the back of a teaspoon.  They were fabulous!  I decided I liked crispy cookies.  The third time I used the basic recipe and added strong coffee to 1/2 of the dough and 1/2 cup chopped Craisins.  They, too were delicious!  I was able to get 60 cookies from each batch.  Thank you so much for posting this recipe.

reviews.review_text: This may just be the perfect cookie recipe. Seriously. I personally prefer doing rounded tablespoon sized cookies, because they are faster and make a nicely sized cookie. I baked them for 10 minutes and they were perfect. They perfectly straddled the line between poofy and flat (if you've tried a lot of cookie recipes you'll know what I mean). I'm so glad I decided to double this recipe, even though I was a tablespoon or two short of butter (which wasn't a problem). Instead of doubling the sugar, I used 1.5 cups, and I did roll them in cinnamon sugar. I can see why these are compared to snickerdoodles, which are favorites of mine, but I think I may prefer these. I added a pinch of nutmeg to round out the flavor without overpowering it - next time I may try 1/4 teaspoon for a doubled batch. I didn't chill for a full two hours, but the dough was fine to work with - I just put the bowl back in the fridge between cookie sheets. Thanks so much for posting!

Great, simple, delicious and gobbled down by my family in minutes. Do make a double batch!

Couple of changes I made due to pantry supplies. I used soft brown sugar and didn't have enough cinammon for the whole recipe so I added powdered ginger and a little bit of cardamon too. YUM! And yielding to my son's demands I added chocolate chips to some of the dough, but did leave most of them free of this ubiquitous ingredient! 

Oh yes, and I didn't read the recipe before coming to the line "refridgerate for 2 hrs", so I didn't, instead spooning on the mixture, and they were just fine.

Enjoy!

attributes.source_text: gobbled down by my family in minutes

When I first saw all the ratings on this recipe, I thought, "How different can a cinnamon cookie be, and why are all these people raving over it? Hasn't everyone had a snickerdoodle?"
Well, it just took one quick batch to see why people are raving over this cookie. Try it...you won't be sorry!

reviews.review_text: My kids gobbled these! We decided they tasted like churros and now there have been requests for the "churro cookies." So not sure if the chilling made the texture better or if it was just the undercooking that helped. Anyway will be saving this one either way for sure!

items.label: Chocolate Chip Muffins
items.name: Chocolate Chip Muffins
items.description: Make and share this Chocolate Chip Muffins recipe from Food.com.
instructions: Preheat oven to 400°F.
Grease twelve muffin cups.
In a large bowl, stir together flour, sugars, baking powder, and salt.
In another bowl, stir together milk, eggs, butter, and vanilla until blended.
Make a well in center of dry ingredients.
Add milk mixture and stir just to combine.
Stir in chocolate chips and nuts.
Spoon batter into prepared muffin cups.
Now bake for 15-20 minutes or until a cake tester inserted in center of one muffin comes out clean.
Remove muffin tin to wire rack.
Cool for 5 minutes.
Remove from tins to finish cooling.
Serve warm or completely cool.
These muffins freeze well.

reviews.review_text: Really great. I used 1 cup wholemeal flour, 1 cup white; and, in a jumbo, american-style muffin tin, this recipe made 6 muffins and took twenty five minutes to bake through. I didn't have chocolate chips or anything so I just cut up a 200g bar of chocolate that really needed using. Delicious! I was really worried that I'd overmixed it but they're very soft. I actually regret that I don't have any other muffin tin as I tried to eat one of these myself and became so stuffed I had to offer the other half away. Only problem I had was that I put in all the wet ingredients and thought I could leave them stand. No. The butter crystallised and I had to stick the bowl they were in into a saucepan that was boiling some water, melt it all over again. Tricky business but, as I say, the muffins are delicious and I can't fault anything.

attributes.source_text: they're very soft

reviews.review_text: So good!! I followed the recipe  and made very few adjustments.  I had a stick of unsalted light butter instead of regular.  I'm glad I did too because it's half the calories and they still tasted buttery and rich.  Also, I used a 6oz of 0% plain greek yogurt instead of milk.  The batter was a might to thick (my fault I added in a bit more flour than I wanted), so I just gently folded in a splash of milk to  make the batter a little more pliable.  I folded in a package of Ghiradelli Semisweet chocolate chips,  but when I make this recipe again, I'll just use half a package.  It really is A TON of chocolate per muffin.  Its good, but a bit much, and I'll be able to make 2 recipes per package of chocolate.

attributes.source_text: they still tasted buttery

reviews.review_text: I am new to making muffins and so I went for a recipe that was right on the top of ratings.  I was not disappointed.  This was super-easy to put together store-cupboard staples and I didn't need a mixer, a real added bonus for me.  As other reviewers the choc chips suspended well and did not sink to the bottom - I did not have as many as I thought though and next time will definitely be adding the full quota as per the recipe for a more chocolatey experience.  My kids loved these and they went down really quickly, next time I will double or triple the recipe and make the individual muffins bigger so I can happily give my kids the muffin and some fruit for Morning Tea (this recipe made 12 muffins on the smaller side).  I froze 6 and am looking forward to grabbing from freezer to lunchbox.  Thanks for a fantastic recipe and I couldn't ask for a better start to my muffin baking.

attributes.source_text: My kids loved these

reviews.review_text: Loved it! I made a few changes, some out of necessity and some based on previous review advice. First, I used all white sugar, as I find brown a little heavy for quick breads. I also halved the chocolate chips as many of you recommended. That worked well so thanks!! I used the specified amount of vanilla and pecans, though, and found it to be just fine. I also doubled the recipe and made one 9x5 loaf pan and three mini-loaves. I cooked the mini loaves at 350 for about 40 minutes and the full-sized loaf for about 55 minutes. Turned out fantastic! (I made loaves because I had the pans prepped for making zucchini bread and then discovered my zucchini was no good, so I searched for a chocolate chip bread, which as it turns out is hard to find without banana. So I tried this recipe and adapted the time and temp and it was great! I'll probably always do the loaves now because I hate cleaning muffin tins! I lined the loaf pans with foil and loved all the crunchy edges with the mini loaves.) Thanks for this recipe!

attributes.source_text: loved all the crunchy edges with the mini loaves

reviews.review_text: These came out well for me. I made pretty close to the recipe, only subbing different chocolate chips. I used semisweet and white chocolate (about 60/40 mix) weighed out to the same total amount called for. I used chopped pecans with them. They are really heavy though! It doesn't affect the taste, and the density is fine, maybe it's just the amount of chips and pecans? Either way, they're a smooth consistency and taste moist and chocolate-y. I don't think the muffin part itself is super sweet, but with that much chocolate added it's a nice balance and I wouldn't want more. Overall, they aren't the best muffins I've ever had, but they still taste good enough to make again. For those who have had issues, I think the butter part might be where some are going wrong. The melted butter needs to cool enough to not start cooking the eggs essentially. I've made the same mistake with a different recipe in the past. I melted mine in the microwave after slicing the stick into thin pieces and then placed it in the fridge while I preheated oven and measure everything else. By the time I got to the butter, I felt the bottom of the dish I melted in to make sure it was barely warm (but the butter still melted) and mixed it into the milk/egg mixture slowly. It mixed well and the end result batter tasted similar to other muffin mixes (not that I tasted it *wink*).

items.label: Baked Salmon
items.name: Baked Salmon
items.description: Make and share this Baked Salmon recipe from Food.com.
instructions: In a medium glass bowl, prepare marinade by mixing garlic, light olive oil, basil, salt, pepper, lemon juice and parsley.
Place salmon fillets in a medium glass baking dish, and cover with the marinade.
Marinate in the refrigerator about 1 hour, turning occasionally.
Preheat oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C).
Place fillets in aluminum foil, cover with marinade, and seal.
Place sealed salmon in the glass dish, and bake 35 to 45 minutes, until easily flaked with a fork.

reviews.review_text: This was sooo beautiful!! I used all fresh including fresh basil (from a container of leaves i have frozen). I was in a rush to make this so i only marinaded them for about 20 mins at most. I also took to the terrific advice of placing them straight in the foil, which is a great time saver. The family loved it and we're making salmon again tonight! This is the first time i've cooked salmon, i've only eaten the smoked kind. I've been searching for a recipe that i can use to try fresh salmon fillets for the first time, and this one is perfect and absolutely no complaints. This marinade also works soooooo WELL with Fresh Unpeeled Prawns (shrimp). I just made some more marinade doubling the recipe. I also used regular extra virgin olive oil which was fine. OMG it was FInger-licking Good. I served them with Fried Fish(silver bream), Fried Eggplant (Augberines), Fresh Salad with Italian Dressing, and Fries. We didnt even eat many Fries as the food was great without it. A Fish Feast Fit for Kings! Yumm!

reviews.review_text:
Great recipe! So easy, and with things that I keep in the house (besides the parsley, for which I substituted dried). My 3 year old son and 8 year old daughters all ate their portions and then started begging for mine. Dh and I both really enjoyed it as well and will definitely make our salmon this way again.

As another reviewer said, I skipped the step of placing the fillets into their own foil packets. I placed the fish (skin down) in the baking dish and poured the marinade over top, then flipped the fish flesh side down in the marinade, covered the dish with plastic wrap and placed in the fridge. It was going to have to stay in the fridge for more than an hour, so after an hour I flipped the fish to skin side down and when I was ready to put it in the oven I used a baster to squirt the marinade over the tops of the fillets and covered the dish with tinfoil and baked it for 30 minutes. It. Was. Perfect!

reviews.review_text:
I made this twice. The first time I followed the recipe exactly. It was highly wonderful. The taste and texture were perfect. The lemon and garlic were in perfect balance, neither overpowering. The olive oil did not make it oily in the least. OK I did add a tad more fresh parsley than called for because I like it, and I get it free from my garden. I didn't bother with aluminum foil, just baked it in the same pyrex glass dish in which I marinaded it, tossing a sheet of foil over the top while it baked. A friend who shared it with me said it was the most flavorful salmon ever. I agree. 

I'm not an intuitive cook. In fact I'm a terrible cook. I can wreck delivered pizza. On the rare occasion I make something edible, good even, it has to be an easy recipe, and a good recipe. This recipe was not only easy, it was REAL easy. And it was not only good, it was REAL good.

The second time I made it I was overconfident and careless. I accidentally poured in too much olive oil, guessed at the measurements of other ingredients instead of measuring, used dried parsley in probably the wrong amount (it was raining. I didn't want to go outside to get fresh parsley), forgot the garlic until I was almost ready to cook it. My worst misake probably was marinading it too long - almost 4 hours. Even with these mistakes it wasn't too bad, kind of oily from too much olive oill, and kind of soft from the long marinade. So learn from my mistakes and do it right. It's worth it.  

Good cooks suggest ways to improve a recipe. I suggested ways to make it worse. Measure once, cut twice. Wait...  This is my first review. I'll get the hang of it.

reviews.review_text: I didn't read the reviews so maybe someone pointed this out already, but 35-45 minutes at 375 is way too long to cook salmon (or probably any fish, unless it is a very thick steak). I ignored my instincts and cooked for 30 minutes (wrapped in foil and then placed in a glass dish) and it was overcooked by a long shot. Salmon should still be pink when cooked, and it should just barely start to pull apart (I wouldn't describe it as flaking in the sense that most white fish flakes). On another site I found that even a 2 inch middle filet (the thickest filet cut on a fish), you can cook it at 400 for 18-20 minutes or, sealed tightly in foil, at a lower temp (350) for about 25-30 minutes. As a rule of thumb, I've seen 10 minutes for each 1 inch of thickness and never bake at 350-375 unless it is wrapped in foil or you'll dry it out (even with some olive oil on it).

I recently made this as a starter for a dinner party, and my wife, who has always detested salmon, because it is too "fishy" absolutely loved it.

I marinated the fish for most of the day, and I dont know if that would have improved the flavour of the salmom, but it certainly didn't seem to do it any harm! You could still taste the Salmon, but it wasn't as overpowering as it can be, and the marinade can be summed up in the same way, you could make out the flavours, but they complimented the Salmon, rather than cancelling it out.

For cosmetic reasons I cut the Salmon fillet into approx. 4" Squares (Before cooking), and served them on a 0.5" thick bed of boiled rice which was slightly larger than the fillet; this helped to keep the fillets hot and also retain moisture - without interfering with the flavour. 
I also added a large (cooked) tiger prawn on top of each fillet - again just for aesthetic reasons, but they do say that half of the tasting is in the seeing!

It was a very easy recipe to make, and tasted fantastic. (And got my wife trying new foods that she would otherwise have avoided)
Thank you.

my wife, who has always detested salmon, because it is too "fishy" absolutely loved it

reviews.review_text: This recipe was very easy, moist, and delicious. Would definitely use again. Changes I made: -Used less olive oil and salt (cut amount in half) -Used dry parsley and minced garlic (came out just as good) and added a little extra of each -Cooked on baking tray covered and lined with foil @ 375 degrees for only 20min (it came out perfect. I would cook it for even less if I want it a little bit more rare next time) -Doubled the marinade with my above changes for 5 filets which were about 1 in thick (used one half to marinade for 1 hour and then the other half I poured on top of the filets before covering and putting them in the oven) Next time, I would add more lemon juice and maybe additional herbs.

attributes.source_text: moist

reviews.review_text:
This was fantastic!  Very good with so little effort. I read EVERY review and decided to use 1/2 tsp. salt and less oil (I used 2 tbsp.).  I put the marinade ingredients in a small bowl and used a whisk to blend.  I used a little less parsley because I only had dried.  I placed a large sheet of foil in a pyrex and added the pieces of salmon and spooned on the marinade and closed up the foil.  I was in a rush to make dinner and didn't have time to let it marinate. It sat with the marinade only until my oven was preheated. After 30 minutes, I opened the foil and broiled it for a little while to brown just a bit.
I'm so glad I tried this recipe.  Thanks for posting and I will certainly make this again!

I am so glad I found this recipe...many years ago on a sailing vacation, I cobbled together something very similar to this as I was trying to bake fish on the boat's mini grill, wrapping the fish in foil so it would steam and stay moist (and not fall through the grill grate!). I used white wine instead of lemon (but I prefer lemon) and I used a white fish. Everyone loved it, as we loved this posted recipe. I agree with the prior reviewer that the balance of ingredients is just right. However, everyone at dinner agreed that salmon doesn't "need" this kind of marinade. Salmon's flavor is very subtle and sort of speaks for itself, and the garlic robs it of that opportunity, but I think this marinade is perfect on any other white fish, especially ocean fish, like snapper or grouper. Next time I use this, it will be on a white fish. Thank you for posting this, it's a keeper!

Nice recipe! I used (1) 14 oz fillet, and checked the foil pack after 25 minutes - wished I had checked after 20 minutes because for my taste, that is probably a closer cook time than the 25 minutes turned out to be. Maybe my oven, maybe being at 7200 feet elevation, maybe my longer marinade time (5 hours instead of 1) which probably precooked the fish like ceviche. I'm betting on the length of marinade to be the culprit. I put marinade and salmon into a tight fitting plastic bag instead of dish as called for, then added fresh cilantro and onion before baking. Capers and slices of carrots, more fresh cilantro, onions, lemon juice topped everything off. I'll be doing this one again!

First time cooking salmon--or really, any fish that didn't come frozen in a box. This recipe was real easy and DH thought it was really good. I marinated the fish in a glass dish and baked it in that dish covered with foil. When I pulled out my cut from the store I had no idea to expect the skin to still be on the fish. After some googling, I marinated and baked it with the skin on. The skin, after cooked, did not alter the flavor or texture of what I was eating. So if you have never cooked fish before this is a good starter recipe!! We don't really like fish but are trying to add more to our diets and, like I said, this was easy and tasted good. Served with steamed veggies and quinoa.

attributes.source_text: DH thought it was really good

reviews.review_text:
Husband says "It's a keeper!" 

Seasonings work well with stronger taste of  "caught" (wild?) salmon. I omitted the fresh parsley & increased amount of fish to serve 4. If you omit the parsley, decrease the salt.
- Marinated in freezer bag (turned bag half way through), baked with center of fish slightly frozen. When placing in baking sheet: place skin side down. If using hand cut fillets and not evenly-thick "steaks" - overlap thinner edges when placing in baking pan. Sealing tin foil tightly  allows fish to steam & stay moist. 
Not a lot of "extra marinade" because of increase in fish but it was still very moist and flavorful.
I can't wait to try recipe grilled over flames!

attributes.source_text: Husband says "It's a keeper!"
it was still very moist

reviews.review_text: We ate this for supper tonight and it was stupendeous! Only thing I did was double the recipe and bake it in the pan I marinaded the fish in (with foil to cover). I didn't have enough basil so I used half the amount asked for. It still tasted wonderful! I love the very slight taste of the lemon on the back of your tongue after you've eaten it. I don't even know if it was the lemon for sure, but whatever it was, it was fantastic!!! We ate this with mashed potatoes and green beans...It is definitely company quality-worthy. I told my husband that since I have most of the ingredients already, the recipe cost me about $7, and that fed 3 people. Can't get that in a restaurant. Thank you for this recipe! We definitely will be using it again and I'll be passing it on to family and friends.

attributes.source_text: We ate this for supper tonight

reviews.review_text: This was good!  As suggested by the other members, I did scale down the oil to 3 Tbsp.  I also added no salt or pepper; instead I did have some Tastefully Simple Garlic Pepper seasoning and also their Garlic Dill Seasoning and added that instead but still adding the crushed garlic as the recipe called for as well as everything else.  I added a few pats of margarine to the top of the fish in the last 5 minutes of baking (baked for 45 minutes).  Next time, I will marinate it for longer than 1 hour, personal preference.  I made this with a 1 lb skinless fillet, with a side of Basmati rice and green beans...great dinner that both my 10 y/o son and I enjoyed!

reviews.review_text: My whole family would give this 10 stars if it were possible, even my 20-month old daughter!  I've never seen her eat salmon like she did tonight.  It was that good.  It had the perfect blend of herb and seasoning.  Salmon can sometimes be a rather fishy fish.  We normally buy the more expensive wild Coho Salmon or something similar.  When that's not available, we buy the farmed salmon and just don't enjoy it as much.  Now, we have a way to enjoy that less expensive farmed salmon!  This was such a hit.  I made with a sun-dried tomato and spinach rice pilaf and "Fried Brussels Sprouts" by CookGirl.  What a fabulous dinner!  Thanks, ngibsonn for such a great, easy recipe.  My husband said it's definitely a Hell's Kitchen-quality dish!  :D  High, high praise.

reviews.review_text: I have now used this recipe about 5 times, and not only on salmon, but on halibut.  My husband and I enjoy it so much that we don't cook the fish any other way!  It is flavorful, perfectly cooked...just delicious!  This last time I used the recipe, I cut down the olive oil from 6T to 3T only because of the fat, and it didn't make any noticeable difference.  Each and every time, I have doubled the amount of minced garlic because we love garlic, and I marinate the fish all day rather than just 1 hour.  Baking the fish in the foil is great....no mess, and the fish does not overcook.  This only takes minutes to prepare and is absolutely delicious!

reviews.review_text: Just finished having this for dinner. Delicious! Clean plates all around. Because of the other comments, I reduced the salt, pepper, and oil a little (by ~1/3). I also cooked it in the pan I marinated it in, covered tightly in foil. I did let it sit out on the counter for 10-15 minutes so it wasn't refrigerator cold when it went into the oven. My filet was perfectly done at 30 minutes. I didn't think the sauce overpowered the salmon at all. I'm a born-and-raised Seattlite, so I grew up on salmon and love it. One of the things I love about it is that it can hold its own with strong flavors like garlic and basil, unlike many other kinds of fish that just take on the flavors of whatever they're cooked with. Will make again and again!
