reviews.review_text: Great!  Making these for a large party next week, so thought I'd give them a trial run.  Concensus around the table was...delicious!  I don't actually eat chicken, so relied on your MANY positive reviews...the marinade/sauce was delicious.  I found I had an abundance of sauce too - might try to precook and drain fat as has been suggested by a few people.  But even without doing that, the sauce that clung to the chicken (I used drumsticks) was flavour enough.  I marinated for 30 mins - will do for longer next time. Thank you!!

DEFINATELY PRE-COOK FIRST.  After reading the glowing reviews-I was so disappointed in the results of this recipe.  They looked so gross-I had a pan of wings floating in a water/sauce and fat-they looked like they had been boiled in ketchup water.  I wish I had paid attention to the other reviews that said to precook them.  I had  made them for a Super Bowl party but thankfully I was able to salvage them-I poured all that liquid off-4 CUPS worth and then whipped up some barbeque sauce and stuck them back in the oven to caramelize.

These were really good wings. I made this batch for the who can't take the heat, and I made a batch of hot wings for the tougher of us. I served these on Superbowl Sunday to rave reviews from the kids.  I'll definately make these again. Ranch dressing was our choice for dipping both the sweet and the hot wings.  I too prebaked all of the wings and poured off the excess grease and then marinated the wings in the sauce for a couple hours prior to finishing them off in the oven.  Thanks Theresa/ Thunderbird, for sharing your great recipe.

attributes.source_text: rave reviews from the kids
I served these on Superbowl Sunday

items.label: Homemade Hamburger Buns (Bread Machine)
items.name: Homemade Hamburger Buns (Bread Machine)
items.description: You will never want to buy hamburger buns again after trying this recipe. Easy to do using a bread machine and so awesome! You can also top rolls with sesame seeds after brushing with melted butter.
instructions: Place all ingredients, except butter, in pan of bread machine according to manufacturer's directions.
Select dough setting.
When cycle is complete, turn out onto floured surface.
Cut dough in half and roll each half out to a 1\
rounds with inverted glass as a cutter.
Place on greased baking sheet far apart and brush with melted butter.
Cover and let rise until doubled, about one hour.
Bake at 350° for 9 minutes.
Note:  Oven temperatures vary so check after 9 minutes to see if done.  Some reviewers baked these anywhere from 12 to 30 minutes.

reviews.review_text:
I have made these rolls twice now. The first time as the recipe said & the second time, I made some changes as others had suggested. I halved the sugar & added 1 1/2 cups wholewheat flour & 2 1/4 white flour - my 14th month old daughter devoured the first batch, so I thought I'd try to make the second batch a bit healthier for her! - I have to say, the first were better than the second. We had the first batch with this BBQ Beef recipe: http://www.slowandsimple.com/Crockpot_Barbecue_Beef_for_Sandwiches-r-727.html & it was fantastic!

For my third attempt, I will just use white flour, but I will still halve the sugar. The wholewheat flour made the rolls a bit spongy I found.

Finally, instead of butter, I brushed them with egg white & sprinkled sesame seeds on the top so we could have them as authentic burger buns. It worked really well. I plan to add some garlic powder & sprinkle them with parmesan cheese next time to see how that would taste with a spaghetti bolognese.

In all a very simple, effective & great recipe you can whip out when you know you've got people coming over but don't have time to get out to the shops! Thanks Marie :0)

attributes.source_text: my 14th month old daughter devoured the first batch

reviews.review_text: Perfect. Delicious. Easy. I made it exactly as the recipe is written. I was a bit confused about whether to add any of the butter to the dough, because it is listed in the middle of the ingredients so logically it seemed to me that it should be added to the dough. The instructions said add everything except the butter to the bread machine, so I did that. I guess the egg adds the fat/oil that I expected would be needed. The butter is just used at the end, melted and brushed on top before the second rise/proof. These babies had great texture and taste. Firm enough to hold a burger with all the trimmings I like to add, yet soft enough to be the perfect accessory. So yummy. I did check my buns after 9 minutes in the oven and decided they needed three minutes more. As the notes at the end of the recipe say, ovens are different so check those buns whilst they are in the oven.

attributes.source_text: Firm enough to hold a burger with all the trimmings
yet soft enough to be the perfect accessory

reviews.review_text: I just made these for the first time today. I'll be making them again. I made 1/2 batch, and baked them on muffin top pans because I wanted the base of the bun to have a "foot". Wow were these easy. Tried to make them sesame seed buns, and while the seeds stick to the melted butter GREAT before you bake them, there's nothing to keep them there when they're done baking. By the time we were eating all the seeds fell off. They proofed in the oven on PROOF setting for a full hour, and baked for 12 minutes at 350. I might consider baking them just a smidge longer to give them a little more color, but there was absolutely nothing wrong with them at 12 minutes. Next time I may consider half the sugar if I'm making them for hamburgers. For pulled pork or bbq's these are the perfect amount of sweet. My next batch is likely to be bratwurst shaped .

attributes.source_text: these are the perfect amount of sweet

reviews.review_text: I just finished my first batch of these buns and they are great.  I used a champagne flute to cut small buns to use for sliders and they came out the perfect size.  Unfortunately I did a couple things wrong as I am new to breadmaking.  First, I overworked my dough a bit as I tried to get as many buns out of it as I could... I shouldn't have mashed the leftover bits together because those buns didn't rise very well.  Secondly, I forgot to brush with butter only to remember it when I noticed there was no browning.  I brushed with butter and baked a little longer only to have the bottoms burn.  I know better now!  I cut the bottoms off and will just use two tops per burger.  I'll definitely use this recipe again and try not to burn anything!  Thanks for sharing Marie :)

I don't know what I can possibly say about these delicious hamburger buns that haven't already been said...  They were easy as pie to throw in the ABM... I was kind of scared since I could NEVER get my breads to rise the 2nd time, but was pleasantly surprised when I saw they rose beautifully.  I did not roll out the dough, but instead portioned the dough into 12 balls, then gently tucked the edges under and slightly rolled them on the board to give them a nice smooth top.  I let them rise in my oven ( which I had pre-heated to 100F just briefly).  They smelled so good while baking and came out golden brown delicious!  We had to sample some and found they tasted just like the yummy yeasty rolls at O'Charley's!  YUM!  These were wonderful as grilled chicken sandwiches...  Tender, soft, with a nice light crust... Never will I buy buns at the store again...  I am forever spoiled!!!  Next challenge will be to try hot dog buns!!!

attributes.source_text: the yummy yeasty rolls
Tender, soft
Tender, soft
with a nice light crust
to give them a nice smooth top

reviews.review_text:
From all of the other reviews, I had some pretty high hopes for this recipe, but I was absolutely floored by how well these turned out.
I was somewhat concerned when I put everything in the bread machine and turned it on, because at first the "dough" was extremely wet.  I was concerned that I had done something wrong, but at the end of the dough cycle, it was more manageable (though still quite sticky).
I used about half whole wheat flour (which turned out great), and forgot to brush the tops with butter (the buns really did not suffer for it, the tops browned beautifully, just were not shiny).  I also took half of the dough, rolled it into smaller dinner-roll sized balls (I think I ended up with about 8 from half of the dough) and put them in a greased pie dish.  I baked those about five minutes longer.  They turned out slightly denser and more moist that way - perfect for a fluffy roll.

attributes.source_text: They turned out slightly denser
more moist that way
perfect for a fluffy roll

reviews.review_text: Everything eventually turned out fine with this dough, but I had a lot of trouble.  I had to use my stand mixer because I needed 2 dozen buns and I used the 1/3 whole wheat flour as suggested in other reviews.  I used less than the total amount of flour in the recipe, but it was very stiff and hard to work with.  I ended up kneading it by hand because it was stalling out my machine.  Then it took much longer to rise than usual (I do usually make all my own bread).  Even the second rise took more than an hour (in the oven with the light on).  I got so nervous that I quickly threw together my icebox rolls recipe that I usually use for buns.  As I said, all turned out well in the end and I had 4 dozen lovely buns (hot dog buns this time).  I actually preferred the texture of these with the whole wheat; but the only guest who asked for the recipe wanted the other one.

I made this recipe exactly as written with no deviations. The taste and texture of this bun is fantastic! I agree that I will probably never purchase store bought buns again. The only reason that I gave this recipe 4 stars instead of 5 is the method concerning rolling out the dough and cutting out the buns, which lead to a flatter bun. I made 6 buns by cutting them out and they turned out flat and not really what I would want in a hamburger bun. The second 6 buns I made by dividing the dough into 6 equal portions and rolling them into a ball. I brushed them with butter and topped with sesame and poppy seeds. The second set came out just like a good hamburger bun should; light, airy, nicely domed and absolutely perfect. I made these for my infamous stuffed bacon blue cheese burgers and the buns I rolled into balls where completely perfect in every way. I also suggest using this same method to make dinner rolls with this recipe. Perfection!

attributes.source_text: light, airy, nicely domed and absolutely perfect
light, airy, nicely domed and absolutely perfect

reviews.review_text: I made these the other day to go along with Recipe #127868 and they came out WONDERFUL!!!!  It was so easy to toss in the bread machine and let it do it's thing.  I took the dough out, divided in half, and using a 3 5/8 inch biscuit cutter, cut them in rounds.  I got 9 large buns but could have gotten at least 14 or so if I had rerolled my scraps out.  I proofed them in my oven and it took a little longer to rise than stated in the recipe but not much.  I baked for about 14 minutes in my convection oven. The buns were so good and LOOKED like burger buns!  This will be my go-to recipe when I need buns for burgers, sloppy joes, barbecue, etc.  Thank you for posting a recipe that I will be using from now on!!!!!

I have made this every night this week(its Thursday), using my black and Decker machine..everyone wants them. I made this with water as my daughter is lactose intolerant and cannot have milk. I did make them once with milk and I find it a lighter bun when water is used..I cut dough in half and then the half in half till I got 8 . Then I formed them into smooth balls. Let rise in a slight warm turned off oven for 30 min..baked for 20..checking on them..tap bottom sounds hollow..Done!<br/>This is a keeper..thank you<br/>ingred went in as follows<br/>water<br/>yeast<br/>sugar<br/>flour<br/>salt <br/>butter<br/>egg<br/><br/>dough setting.

attributes.source_text: I find it a lighter bun when water is used

reviews.review_text: thankyou for this recipe...these are great. Ran across this looking for a recipe to replace my husbands spongy/airy buns he likes to eat his sandwiches on from the store hoping he would switch to a more healthy bun and he really likes them....funny thing is I have been using them as bread too after searching with no luck for a bread recipe that doesn't crumble on me half way through the loaf.... I toast them in the morning, make PBand J and make grilled cheese with them (my children love them this way better than bread) I love that I can play with the recipe too....like  I used honey instead of sugar and I swithed the 3 3/4 C, flour to 1 1/2 C WW flour, 1 1/2 C. unbleached flour and 3/4 C. quick oats..they are perfect...I will keep it this way as I like a more whole grain bun. Thanks again  2 problems solved  in one recipe.

attributes.source_text: he really likes them
my children love them this way better than bread

reviews.review_text: These were very nice! I normally use bread machine yeast in my maker but my husband had fortunately (I guess) bought active-dry this last time and I wasn't sure how these would turn out since I thought you were supposed to proof active-dry? Anyway I just dumped it all in no proofing and these turned out excellent. I got 12 slider sized buns out of this with a bit of dough leftover so I just made 3 bonus rolls. The last few mins of baking I rubbed butter on the tops and sprinkled sesame seeds over, that was when they turned golden on top! Sliced each one and these took our st. paddy's day guinness burgers http://www.food.com/recipe/guinness-burgers-22210 over the top! Thanks!!

Great! I halved this recipe and got 5 large buns. My bread machine dough cycle includes time to rise, and I was uncertain if I should let the dough rise once before shaping the rolls, so I actually took the dough out before the cycle finished, shaped my buns and let them rise that way. My rise time was closer to 2 hours as a result.  Next time, I'll try the double-rise technique. These have a very non-yeasty, slightly sweet taste to them.  Like a better version of store bought buns. I subbed 1/3 of the flour with AP so they would be as soft as possible and it worked very well.  Before baking, I brushed with a mixture of 1 beaten egg w/ a tsp of water for a golden, shiny top!

attributes.source_text: slightly sweet taste
very non-yeasty
as soft as possible

reviews.review_text: This is the best recipe for hamburger buns. I have tried quite a few. They were a big hit with my husband and his golf buddies. I used almond milk and 1 teaspoon of salt instead of 3/4 tsp. I used an egg wash instead of butter, right before the rolls went into the oven. I thought 1/4 cup of sugar would be too much, but it is perfect. I let the rolls rise for one hour. I put a pan of hot water on the bottom shelf of the oven, while the oven was preheating and left it, until the rolls were done baking. (I do this with my bread, so, I figured, why not) They were done in 11 minutes. Perfect...really delicious. This is my new recipe, I am deleting all others from my "favorites".

attributes.source_text: They were a big hit with my husband and his golf buddies
They were a big hit with my husband and his golf buddies

reviews.review_text: This recipe was easy enough to put together, but for me and my family, it was way too sweet for hamburger buns.  Rolling out I found to be a waste of time, really.  I did roll them and cut them as directed, but found it was just as effective to divide the dough and shape into buns.  For home made I would've liked a tad bit more yeast as well.  Overall, we did enjoy these and it was fantastic having them hot like the meat patties.  (My cooktime ended up being 20 minutes).  I will be making them again and again, but I will cut the sugar in half (for starters) and increase the yeast by 1/4 t. increments until I get it the way that I prefer it.  Thank you so much for sharing! :)

Yum!

These were outstanding!  I followed the directions exactly, with no substitutions and the finished result is wonderful!  The only thing I wondered about was the butter, the recipe states 2 tbsp butter, which I added to the bread machine, but then the recipe states to brush with melted butter (which I did, with extra butter), so I was sort of worried that I did it wrong.  Regardless if the butter was supposed to go in the dough or just on top of it, they turned out so delicious!  I can't wait to serve tonights hamburgers on these buns!  Definitely a keeper and I will be making these again soon.  Thank you for a wonderful recipe.

These are awesome!! I'm so happy I found it on my quest to match my grandmother's recipe. It's the closest I've ever seen to my grandmother's recipe. Hers were still a little bit more airy, so I'm wondering if she added some vital gluten to hers. It was the exact same taste though! I made these for hot beef sandwiches for supper, and have already eaten 2 plain! My grandmother used to use her bun recipe to make what she called kolache. It was either a prune or apricot filled bun (not the normal kolache), but no one ever could get the recipe down perfectly because she did them off of a chicken scratch recipe. You don't know what finding this recipe really means to me! I will be able to carry on a family favorite!! Thank you Marie! You even have my grandmother's name...

attributes.source_text: I made these for hot beef sandwiches for supper

reviews.review_text: This was the first time I'd ever made rolls with my bread machine!  They turned out really well.  I made a slow cooker pot roast dip and used these as our rolls.  My boyfriend ate 4 of them and used one as a dessert roll (peanut butter, honey and bananas)... even though I added italian seasoning to these rolls ;). These reheat really well when slit open and toasted on a flat top. I rolled these out to about 1/2" which tasted great and are about the size of the thinner flat buns that are sold in stores now.  We added sesame seeds to a few also which turned out great! I'm going to make them mega sized next time!  LOVE this recipe, thank you so much!

attributes.source_text: My boyfriend ate 4 of them

reviews.review_text: I am spoiled now! This was the easiest most successful bread baking recipe I have ever used. And the results Came out absolutely perfect and delicious. I am sheltered in because of the coronavirus. I had hamburgers but no buns and no store had them either. I woke up in the middle of the night and said I can make them myself and found this recipe. It gave me a feeling of power and strength to not complain but do something about being Bun-less. So I got up this morning and made magnificent soft cushy buns! Thank you so much for this recipe The results are so delicious I can’t keep my mouth off of my buns!

items.label: Perfect Turkey in an Electric Roaster Oven
items.name: Perfect Turkey in an Electric Roaster Oven
items.description: I never found good information on making a great whole roasted turkey in an electric roaster oven and thought I'd share my tried and true tips for making your holiday turkey moist and beautiful and delicious!  I've read that roaster ovens effectively 'steam' the turkey making the meat come out ... well, steamed.  This is not true. Follow these tips and your holiday turkey will get rave reviews!
instructions: Take the insert pan out of the roaster and pre-heat the roaster to its highest setting. On mine it's 450, but use 500 if your oven goes that high.

Do not wash the turkey!  The USDA says that washing it could cause a spread of salmonella poisoning.  Sprinkle salt in the cavities. Stuff if desired.  Don’t pre-stuff your turkey; mix and stuff ingredients immediately before roasting. Tossing in a few pieces of cut fruit or herbs is not considered 'stuffing.'  Stuffing usually means filling up the cavity with about ¾ cup stuffing per pound of turkey.

Rub the entire bird with olive oil or butter. Doctor up your bird with whatever special seasonings you wish.  I always use poultry seasoning. Finish with a good sprinkle of seasoning salt and black pepper.

I highly recommend using a wired thermometer so you can watch the temperature without lifting the lid.  Your turkey will be done much earlier than the estimated cook time, so keep a sharp eye on that thermometer.  If using a pop-up turkey plug type thermometer, those little pop-ups stick sometimes so you should really use two of them.

Put the rack into the insert pan and make sure the handles are up, not tucked below.  Put the bird in the insert pan on top of the rack.  Don’t add water to the pan. Put the insert pan back into the roasting pan.  If your roaster doesn't have an insert pan, it's ok - just be very careful putting the bird into that hot oven, you don't want to burn your hands on the sides of the oven! Cover.
Roast at highest setting for 30 minutes.  The butter/oil, seasonings and the searing time will make the skin beautifully browned and perfect!
After 30 minutes, turn the oven temperature down to 325.

The turkey will self-baste if you do not lift the lid, so you don't have to baste it every 20 minutes like you do in your conventional oven. DO NOT LIFT LID during cooking time!  Lifting the lid will increase cooking time because roaster ovens lose their heat unlike regular ovens.   I've read that roaster ovens effectively 'steam' the turkey making the meat come out  --  well, steamed.  This is not true as you will find out.  Similar to the roasted chickens you can get at your supermarket, the bird will come out moist and perfectly roasted.  Why do you think they call it a Roaster Oven?.
Figure your total cooking time from the time you first put the bird in the roaster.  The Butterball website has a great calculator:
http://www.butterball.com/calculators-and-conversions.
FINAL TEMPERATURE FOR SAFETY AND DONENESS IS: 180 DEGREES IN THIGH AND 165 DEGREES IN BREAST AND STUFFING. Juices should be clear, not pink.

Check your turkey EARLY.  Really start watching the temp an hour before it's supposed to be done. Your turkey will almost certainly be done before the suggested cooking time.  Watch your wired meat thermometer.  If using a pop-up turkey plug type thermometer, check by lifting the lid quickly so the oven doesn’t lose its heat.  If necessary, check after another 30 minutes, but I doubt you'll have to do that.  I say check after 30 minutes because it's really OK to let the bird roast a little extra - you won't dry it out using my method if you let it go for 1/2 hour.
When done, remove the turkey from the roaster, tent with foil, and let rest for 20 minutes.  This allows the juices to really seep into the meat, so they say.
If you try this method, please let us know your results!
Happy Thanksgiving everyone!

reviews.review_text: I was super nervous about this. I started with a 16 lb turkey and old roaster. Turkey was thawed 4 days, although there was a tad of ice still on it when we started taking all the stuff out. It was a Kroger brand one that had a solution in it, so I didn't bribe it just took it out and went ahead with the recipe. I used butter, and put as much as I could on the turkey, over and under skin. Then I used a spice recipe that I found (somewhere, if I remember I'll come back and edit, but it was a basic turkey spice with sage) and put it on the outside and under the skin. The recipe I found for stuffing the cavity was an onion (quartered), a bunch of thyme, and a head of garlic (halved) and one half of a lemon. I fit about half that in my turkey. I preheated the roaster while I fixed up the turkey, then put it directly in. For my case, the skin touched the sides but didn't burn so I didn't put the foil. I had put a wired thermometer in, and at the 30 min mark it said 140. Well I knew that wasn't right, so I reinserted it and bumped the roaster to 325 per the recipe. I kept having the same issue with the thermometer until I realized that the temp probe was pushed by the roasting pan lid. We were never able to get the temp probe to do right, so we ended up having to open the lid to check the temp with an instant read. I'm a little particular about this, so we did it every 15 min or so once we got to a close point. When it hit 160 (I believe that was 2 hours into cooking, 40 min at a high of 450 and 1 1/2 hours at 325) we took it out and I took a stick of butter and rubbed it again. Then I put it under the (already preheated) broiler for 10 or so minutes (my friends said they could smell it and were worried t was burning so I took it out, not sure exactly how long). I rested it 30 min on the pan it came out of the oven in with a tinfoil tent, and then we transferred it to the table. It was another 20 min until we ate, and if I could redo the night I would have put the tinfoil back on it and a towel to keep it warmer. It was still great though!! And it was a beautiful turkey, super moist and I got a lot of compliments on it!! I couldn't be happier with how this turkey came out!

attributes.source_text: super moist

reviews.review_text: I posted some of the following as a comment to someone else's review but I figure most people will not see it there. . I cooked a 20# bird in my new electric roaster yesterday. I initially set it at 450*F for 30 minutes and then 325*F for the rest of the time. I figured on 4-5 hours total time. I decided to give it a quick check with my instant read thermometer after 3 hours. The breast was already at 201*F! I checked it in 5-6 spots. That thing was probably done in 2 1/2 hours or less. I saved the meal by FTC (foil, towel, cooler) for 2 1/2 more hours until time to carve. It turned out well and very moist and flavorful and all the guests commented on how well it tasted. Wow, these roasters sure cook things fast. . My guess on the fast cook time is perhaps the marinade I injected it with added some steam to speed things up. Also, I added a can of chicken broth to the bottom of the pan, which probably added even more steam. I did not remove the lid prior to checking the temp at 3 hours. . I did rinse the turkey off with cold water before injecting it and putting it in the roaster. This is the only site I read where it said to not do that. 4-5 other sources said to rinse and pat dry. After thawing in the fridge for 5 days, a lot of red juices ran out when I unwrapped it in the sink and I didn't want any of that residue to be left in or on the turkey. . Maybe next time I'll change the cooking temp to 275 instead of 325. I plan on checking the accuracy of the roaster temp with a wired thermometer before then. I opted not to use it during the cooking because I didn't want the wire to leave a gap between the lid and roaster and let heat and moisture escape.

attributes.source_text: very moist
all the guests commented on how well it tasted

reviews.review_text:
Wow, this recipe looked so simple I went out and bought an electric roaster to give it a try for Thanksgiving this year!

This is the first time I have ever cooked a turkey, so I think we will call this the year of calibration. ;-)

I purchased an Oster 18 Quart roaster from Target, highest heat setting is 450, so I used that for the first 30 minutes, then re-set it to 325.

I had a 14.54 pound bird, unstuffed. I did put a few clementines, washed and halfed, in it. We let it thaw for 72 hours in the fridge.

We were aiming for turkey on the table at 2PM, so we put it in at 9AM, to allow for 30 minutes of resting, and 30 minutes of "oops, it isn't done, keep it in there an extra 30 minutes," and about 15 minutes to carve.

Checked it at 3 hours, 30 minutes and it was done - I think over done. I'm glad I checked it 15 minutes earlier than the USDA chart recommended!

It ended up pretty dry, but I think that's because we left it resting for well over an hour instead of 30 minutes. I'll time it better next year, and probably check it around 2.5 hours or 3 hours. I also intended to get a thermometer with a cord, but forgot. I definitely will get one before I cook another turkey since I can't see inside my roaster without lifting the lid.

Overall, this was a great "first turkey" experience! The turkey looked beautifully browned. We put butter, salt and pepper, and a little rosemary on top.

I will definitely use this recipe again!!

attributes.source_text: for Thanksgiving this year

reviews.review_text: As we approach the holidays, just wanted to come here and say THANK YOU for this recipe. I've used this for 6 years and I shudder to remember the turkeys that came before it. I've done brined, unbrined, stuffed, unstuffed, fresh, and previously-frozen turkeys and they all came out great (I think it works better with unstuffed though). The key is the wired thermometer and paying attention to the temperature/cooking time, because it WILL be done sooner than you think! After the first 30 minutes on high + about an hour at 325, I always find myself turning the roaster down bit by bit so that it doesn't cook too fast and throw off my serving time. Also if I'm not able to tuck the wing tips under the bird, I usually wrap them in foil after the first 30 minutes so they don't burn. My go-to method now is the cooking instructions from this recipe + Ina Garten's roast turkey recipe + about 1/2 inch (or less) of sherry in the bottom of the roasting pan. I have trouble getting the skin to brown in my roaster so I add butter under the skin too. I like to pre-infuse the butter the the night before with whatever spice/herb blend I'm using and then before cooking I'll rub it inside the cavity, under the skin, and melt the rest to brush on top. The extra butter + sherry usually means I have enough fantastic drippings for gravy. This recipe saved me (and my loved ones) from years of dry turkeys. I threw away the instructions that came with the turkey roaster and use this religiously in its place. BIG THANKS to the author!

This step by step was good, but not perfect. I think there are a LOT of variables that impact cook time/how it cooks - so unless you are doing every single thing EXACT to the above instructions (including size), be prepared to get varying results. All and all it worked out great, but there were some touch and go moments there when it was cooking INSANELY quick. I cooked a FRESH turkey, almost exactly 15lbs in the Rival Roaster Oven with Self-Basting Lid from Walmart. I liquid brined it the night before starting at 10PM in the fridge. Took it out of fridge around 2PM on cooking day, to bring it to room temperature before putting in the roaster. While the roaster pre-heated at the highest temp, I dried the entire turkey with papertowel, added the aromatics into the cavity (not stuffing), and smothered the entire bird in garlic butter. LOTS of garlic butter. I placed the bird in the roaster, inserted the wired thermometer into the meatiest part of the breast - make sure you are not touching bone. I roasted it on the highest temperature for 30 minutes as instructed, and then put the temperature down to 325. I noticed the temperature raising VERY fast. I expected it to take about 2-2.5 hours, and 30 minute resting time. However, it got to around 130/140 after only an hour. I did open the lid at this point to double check my thermometer was properly placed. At this point, the sides of the birds were a nice golden brown but the whole body looked steamed/boiled. I didn't panic because I knew I could broil it. But this was the first time I lifted the lid was I was surprised to see it wasn't all browning up like the recipe describes. I decided to check my thermometer using heavily iced water. It was supposed to read around 32 but it was reading closer to 44. So, knowing my thermometer read a little high I kept a SUPER close eye on it and gave a bit of wiggle room for the breast temperature to hit 175. It hit 175 about an hour and a half into cooking (maybe a bit less). It was honestly SO fast - my mom and my aunt couldn't believe it. So, I decided to take it out at that point. I put it into a disposable roaster tray and tented it with tinfoil. At this point the body was still not browned at all. It was still completely white. After about 45 minutes of being tented, I turned on the oven broiler at 500, smothered it with more butter, and put it under the broiler. I did keep the meat thermometer into it while it was tented as to not let the temp drop below 140. It stayed quite warm the whole time. I left the turkey under the broiler for about 20-25 minutes and the skin crisped right up! After broiler, I took it out, and let it sit (again tented) for 20 minutes, and then it was ready to carve. It tasted AMAZING. Juicy and flavourful, and crispy in the right places. Due to all the tweaking, I would say this recipe is OK-good for cooking instructions. Again, if I was following it to a T, I could have have a different outcome, but I don't know that it would have resulted it in being brown all over as suggested. I am pretty confident in the kitchen and am fine to troubleshoot with little stress, but if you are not, you likely would have panicked at the sight of your white turkey and it being done an hour or more before you expected. I was happy to have this as a guideline though, and it was one of the better ones I found in my research. Happy to know what works for my roaster and what doesn't now. It did make a large amount of drippings that were awesome for the gravy!

attributes.source_text: Juicy and flavourful
crispy in the right places

reviews.review_text: I had never cooked a whole turkey in an electric roaster and was apprehensive about the process.  I cooked it for a community group's Christmas party.  The group had purchased the turkey.  It was a 13.75# turkey with a pop-up thermometer.  I followed this recipe exactly except I mixed the melted butter with browning sauce (roaster manufacturer tip) in place of the seasonings mentioned in the recipe.  I did salt the cavity.  I had to leave the roaster after I turned the heat down to 325 degrees.  I arrived back to check the turkey 3 1/4 hours after beginning the roast.  The pop-up thermometer had popped.  My thermometer read slightly above 185 for the breast and 180 for the thigh.  The skin was beautifully browned and pulled away from the body near the thigh.  I followed the turkey carving video also on this site.  The turkey was absolutely perfect!  Moist and aesthetically pleasing.  To serve the turkey, I prepared a large slow cooker by inserting the roasting rack and then lining the slow cooker with foil above the rack.  I put the carved turkey in the slow cooker in the same pattern as was suggested in the video when using a platter.  Upon arrival at the party site, I added a little water below the foil in the slow cooker and turned it on to low.  Worked wonderfully and gathered compliments!

attributes.source_text: Moist and aesthetically pleasing

reviews.review_text: I’d bought a roaster oven last year and wondered why my turkey didn’t brown or look done. It was cooked and tasty, but was not very pretty. So this year, I’ve gotten smarter and searched online. So glad to have found your recipe! Loved your suggestions and clear explanation. I’d put butter under the skin and slathered butter all over the outside of the bird, then sprinkled with minimal seasonings. The turkey turned out beautifully and was so golden brown, my picture doesn’t due it justice! The only snag was that I couldn’t find the Butterball cooking times/conversions, so followed my roaster oven time guide, but should’ve cooked it probably 15/30 minutes longer, but other than that, the juices simply poured right out of it, it was amazing!!! It was an 8.9 ounce turkey, and the total time it was in the roaster including the seating at the beginning, was 2 hours. My roaster oven guide suggested 1-3/4 hours. And I read your advice that cooking it longer would not dry it out, but in all of the cooking excitement, I took it out. It did register 180 degrees, but a few minor places needed more cooking, which we took care of. Perhaps I overstuffed it! We always buy a Lil’ Butterball, it’s just for the four of us. Next year, I’ll be smarter, but this was still my best turkey ever! Thank you for the wonderful recipe!

attributes.source_text: the juices simply poured right out of it

reviews.review_text: So I have had a Turkey Roaster for a couple years now... and never used it. It is the GE one that goes to 450. I followed the instructions pretty much as stated. Our turkey was only a 5.1Kg (about 10.5 lbs) And it was done in two hours. I stuffed it with onions and apples, and seasoned it with Poultry seasoning and Essence (the Bam! stuff) on the inside. Rubbed it down with oil and Essence'd the outside. http://www.food.com/recipe/emerils-essence-5031 Have to say that this was one of the best turkeys I have ever done. Normally I season some butter and put it under the skin, but I simply didn't need to. Bird was -Completely- Thawed when cooking began and I didn't pre-heat the oven. Stuck it in for about 40 minutes on 450, then turned down to 325. I don't trust those pop up things. So I used my normal corded thermometer. And when she hit 165-170, I shut it off. Allthough it only took two hours and we were having supper a bit early, I will know for next time to time it better. (Have a second turkey that is awaiting my attention in a few months. :P) But thanks so much for the guidelines. Recipe will be used again and again!

Oh Em Gee - I will not cook another turkey in the big oven - from now on it's going in the roaster oven! I've cooked many a turkey in my 59 years and I have to say, this one was awesome. The ONLY thing it lacked was more crispy brown skin, but there was enough, on the parts closest to the oven walls, to keep me happy. The meat was so moist and tender and yet pulled right away from the bones.

I followed the instructions pretty much as given, putting one halved onion and one halved lemon in the cavity. I used olive oil, garlic salt, a little crushed dried thyme, and some coarsely ground black pepper for seasoning. Started it at 450* (as high as my roaster goes) and set a timer for 30 minutes, then turned down to 325* and set the timer for 3 hours and 30 minutes, for my unstuffed 18 pound bird.

Well I did check it after 3 hours and that sucka was DONE! Checked it in several spots with my instant-read thermometer and it was cooked through, and the meat pulling away from the leg bones. Since it was only 4 pm, I turned off the roaster, sucked out some of the wealth of luscious juice so the turkey wasn't sitting in it (it had risen very slightly above the rack) and let it sit til we were ready to eat about 5:15. I made the best gravy with that juice from the pan too.

DH who LOVES his turkey asked me to please come in here and give highest praise to Squirrel Gone Wild on this one! THANK YOU!

reviews.review_text: WONDERFUL!  I've used the roaster oven before...well, I tried but I was being supervised by family and being told how everyone else would do it.  This year, we're spending Thanksgiving at my parent's with my brother's family as well so I am off turkey duty.  The problem, of course, is my husband and I could happily live off the leftovers for a year and we won't have any.  So I did what any good wife would do...I bought two turkeys, one for July and the other for today. so I can have the meat in the freezer ready to be thawed for sandwiches.  <br/>Anyway, I had a small turkey (10.45 lbs) and followed the directions here to a tee, save one step.  I preheated at 450.  I covered my turkey in both olive oil and margarine, seasoned salt, pepper and poultry seasoning.  I took the neck and giblets and through them in the crockpot to simmer with carrots, onions, and celery to make stock and cook the giblets for stuffing.  I screwed up a little and preheated the roaster with the pan still in it.  Put the turkey on the rack and lowered it into the hot oven, covered it and left it on 450 for 1/2 hour.  I dropped it to 325 at that time and set the timer for 3 hrs and 15 mins.  I do not have a meat thermometer and the turkey didn't come with a popper, so I was using faith alone.  At 3hrs and 10 mins, I opened the lid.  The skin had come back from the legs so I knew it was done.  I turned it off and covered it and let it sit for 1/2 hour.<br/>I have used cooking bags, brined or 24 hours and basted to where my fingers were sore and this is one o the most tender, moist turkeys with crispy skin I have ever had/made!!  I was so surprised the skin got crispy!  I loved using the oven bags, but talk about no crispy skin.  This was just awesome!  Thank you!! (BTW, I didn't put any liquid in at all and due to using the rack, nothing was stuck on.  Clean up was a breeze)

reviews.review_text: This Thanksgiving was the first time I've cooked in a turkey in a long, long time.  My wife has always cooked the turkey in our roaster and she assured me it was real easy.  She said look on the internet find you a recipe and go from there. While cutting out coupons I found a recipe for brine using soy sauce.  I put the 16 lb turkey in the brine for 16 hours.  I followed the directions here as suggested.  I preheated the roaster on the highest setting,  Greased the bird down with olive oil.  Filled up the bird with stuffing and placed it in the roaster on the highest setting for 30 minutes.  Turned it down to 325 degrees as suggested.  Put it on the timer for 4 hours.  I didn't take the cover off once to check it.  Now I was reluctant and worried that the turkey wasn't going to be done or not cooked right.  I mean this was the first time cooking a turkey in quite some time.  OK folks the bird was PERFECT! The meat fell right off the bone.  The breast meat was flavorful, tender and juicy.  I was totally impressed how easy this was, (just as my wife said),  I highly recommend using this recipe.  I'd also suggest brine before cooking the bird.  You can't go wrong with this one.

reviews.review_text: My oven went out this year (still had the stovetop) and could put the broiler on quickly to keep things warm in there. So instead of getting a new element I bought a turkey roaster (rival) $24.00 what a deal!  I have never been a good turkey maker and was also concerned because I needed to make it Gluten, Dairy and yeast free.  I found this recipe and bought a 16-20 pound GF butterball.  I turned it up to 450 and while it heated up, I olive oiled it, salt & peppered it like crazy.  Stuffed it with onion, celery, carrots, honey-crisp apples, lemons and a few leaves of sage.   It didn't have popper timer on it and I didn't have any string to tie the wings either.  Oh well, in it goes and the searing sound it made when that floppy bird went in there scared me to death!  So I hurried and put a little water in the bottom and closed the lid.  Then I thought I was going to steam it to death!  Yes, I was nervous.  Then I smell burning turkey.  It says to NOT lift the lid, but I didn't have a choice!  I lifted it and realized that it was the wings hanging and touching the edge of the roaster that was burning the skin, so I tucked some foil down the sides and put the lid back on.  About 30 minutes later, I'm sorry, I just couldn't resist to look because I was still smelling a little burning, so I lifted the lid and checked and it looked fine, the legs and half the turkey was browning nicely, so  I turned it down to 325 set the lid and figured I 'll just leave it and hope for the best.  I thought perhaps because I lifted the lid twice I would have to add on a little time.  Its 11:00AM.  Out at 2:00PM  Rest time and dinner at 3:00.    30 min for the 450 temp and 2 1/2 at 325.  total 3 hrs.  At 2:00 I looked and well, breast bone was sticking out!  The breasts where splitting away from each other!  It was a nice brown, not burnt, I am sure I overcooked it.  I put a meat thermo in that bird all over the place and it registered way to high.  Definitely dry turkey.  I pulled the bone right out, took my hands and just grabbled those breasts and pulled them off.  Cut it into slices and pulled the legs and rest of bird apart and put on a plate. OMG!!!!!!  That bird was THE BEST turkey I have EVER made in my life.  I am almost 50, have made a lot of birds in my years.  It wasn't overcooked at all, was juicy, tender, browned.  Monday after Thanksgiving. I figure definitely last day for eating turkey, mad a soup with the little leftovers we had.  STILL was tender NOT dry at all.  OMG!  Everyone complimented me on dinner.  TRY THIS, you won't regret it.  I will NEVER do a turkey in an oven again.  NEVER.  Besides it leaves the whole oven for other stuff.  :):)

reviews.review_text: I will start by saying I did not take the lessened cook time seriously enough, especially since I decided to drop my temp to 300 degrees rather than 325 after the initial heat blast (figured it would give the skin more time to crisp). By all accounts I was anticipating a 3.5 - 4 hour roast for my 24.6 pound bird, rather than the 5-6 hours I'd have it in the full size oven. My turkey was done in exactly 2 hours using my 18 qt. Oster roaster oven. I was also able to make 4 cups of gravy with the drippings. I prepare my bird slightly differently, adding some butter and preferred seasoning blend under the skin as well. The skin split wide open over the breast sometime during the first hour, total bummer but the meat did not get dry at all. I was using a corded thermometer, so that was the only time I lifted the lid to check and baste (I was already at 120 degrees, and coming up in temp very quickly.. concern about my thermometer placement finally got the best of me and I had to check). At the end, most of the skin was beautifully cooked and crispy'ish. Very pleased with this method, thank you so much for sharing it!

reviews.review_text: Thank you thank you thank you!!  This was my first time cooking a turkey ever.  My wife refused to change the basting oil that I hated so she said either I make the turkey or suck it up.  So, I made it.  And WOW, it was the BEST turkey BY FAR that our family has ever had!  I heard good things about a roaster oven so I bought that and found this recipe.  Thank you all for the reviews as well, it built my confidence up.  Plus when it was done everything fell off the bone and SO EASY to carve compared to a regular oven!  And it freed up the oven to boot.  It's the ONLY way to go, I can't thank you enough!  The only hard thing about it is not being able to see the turkey for 3 hours, but it's awesome when you pop and lid and see how great it looks.  I had a 13 pound turkey and cooked for 3 total hours.  When I checked the temperature of the breast it was 200 degrees, so it probably could have cooked less, but it did NOT affect the taste or juiciness of the bird, it was still the best we've ever had. reviews.review_text: I don't think you can stress enough how fast a turkey cooks in a roaster. This was my first roaster experience. I followed the instructions exactly, starting at 450 for 30 minutes and then turning down to 325. I cooked a 23 lb. fresh turkey unstuffed (from a local farm) in 2 hours and 20 minutes. I knew it would cook fast, but didn't expect THAT fast. I used an external digital thermometer which was very accurate. When it went off at 185 it was definitely done, though we also confirmed the temp in a few other spots with an instant read thermometer. We turned the roaster down to 200, and let it sit for 2+ hours until our guest arrived, basting it now and then. It was perfect and very moist looking, browned on the sides but not so much on the top, which OK with me. That said, I am a vegetarian and can't vouch for the taste, but my guests said it was very juicy and tender and tasted.great. Another HUGE plus is that using a roaster for the bird freed up the oven for reheating all the veggies I made the day before. I can't see doing a turkey in the oven ever again. Cleanup was also pretty easy this morning after leaving it to cool in the garage overnight.

reviews.review_text: I made a turkey in my electric roaster once before, but Googled cooking it that way to get ideas. After reading the directions here, I bought a digital thermometer so I wouldn't have to open the lid. We cooked a 19-1/2 lb. Butterball turkey. It should have taken about 4-1/5 to 5 hours. However, the turkey was done in about 3 hours according to the temperature on the thermometer (my roaster's highest temperature is 450 degrees). We let it rest for about 1/2 hour. Although the top didn't brown as much as I would have liked, it was delicious. So, just a reminder, as suggested here, make sure you check the turkey well before the time it is supposed to be finished. I made a note on the guide that came with my roaster so next year I'll know to have the sides heated to coincide with the bird being cooked. Kind of had to rush through that because the bird was done an 1-1/2 hrs. before I thought it would be. It was the first time we never basted a turkey. This is so much easier than using the oven and going into it numerous times to baste. Also, it leaves the oven available to cook and/or heat up the side dishes.

Dry. No real flavor. This was my second time using my roaster and second time it was dry. First time I totally overcooked it so this time I watched it like a hawk. Had a 16 lb pre brined fresh turkey. Rubbed an olive oil, butter and fresh herbs mixture inside, under the skin and on top, put cut up orange, Apple and celery inside (forgot the onion, didn't have carrot). Half hour at 450, 1.5 hours at 325. Wasn't ready yet. Checked another half hour later, ready! Temps were very high in thigh and breast. Set aside covered with foil to rest. Had a very dry bird. I will try this ONE more time but I'm going to season a little heavier and add broth and wine in the pan. I want to do the bacon on the breast trick but I also like to keep my variables low. I'm going to try it with a small bird for a weekday meal so I'm not wasting big birds at holiday time. Had a lot of drippings for gravy but I bought gravy since my last attempt was also horrible. I'm usually a decent cook, especially with a recipe to follow. My new oven has 2 sections and one is a convection oven. Might just have to use that and rotate sides in the top half. I'm still disappointed. Sigh.

Well let me tell you my day has not gone well.  I was up late.  Got up early to find my 20lb. Turkey would not fit in my roasting pan.  I have company coming in 6 hours.   Then I remembered we have an electric 16 qt roaster in the garage.  Thank god.   Well it does not end there.  I get the turkey ready but 2 hours into cooking I realize I didn't put in the rack because it was in the cupboard (not a good idea to keep things seperate)  my husband helped me by pulling the turkey up and I put the rack below.   We had a hard time figuring out where to stick the thermometer so I am checking it the old fashioned way the drumstick. Ok so now I read one of these reviews and he said that they put the turkey in the oven to brown it a little more so im going to do that.  The drumsticks move easily and its been cooking 4 1/2 hrs.  Even though we had to open the lid a couple of time.  Now it looks a little dry but we will see.  Wish I had seen this website.   So now dinner is over and it was a success wasn't dry was really good and moist and most of all I will always use the electric roaster oven for thanksgiving/christmas or any holiday that requires me to cook a big piece of meat.

The only thing I would have done differently because my roasting lid was a little warped (lid didn't fit properly )I should have used a little foil to close some of the gaps. I’m over 50 from a line of excellent cooks. First time I’ve ever used roaster without wine and broth in bottom of pan. First time I’ve ever over cooked a turkey. items.label: Old-Fashioned Banana Cream Pie
items.name: Old-Fashioned Banana Cream Pie
items.description: Before Cool Whip and instant pudding, this was how a cream pie was made. If you leave out the bananas, you have vanilla cream pie. If you add 1 cup shredded coconut to milk as it's being heated, you have coconut cream pie.
instructions: Have baked 9-inch pie shell ready.
In a large saucepan, scald the milk.
In another saucepan, combine the sugar, flour and salt; gradually stir in the scalded milk.
Over medium heat, stirring constantly, cook until thickened.
Cover and, stirring occasionally, cook for two minutes longer.
In a small bowl, have the 3 egg yolks, slightly beaten, ready; stir a small amount of the hot mixture into beaten yolks; when thoroughly combined, stir yolks into hot mixture.
Cook for one minute longer, stirring constantly.
Remove from heat and blend in the butter and vanilla.
Let sit until lukewarm.
When ready to pour, slice bananas and scatter in pie shell; pour warm mixture over bananas.
If desired, make a meringue (you'll have 3 leftover egg whites) to top the pie, or just let the pie cool until serving.

reviews.review_text: Whew! This recipe is DECEPTIVELY difficult!!! I just finished baking and the longest part was incorporating the scalded milk into the flour mixture-it took 37minutes!! The first time I messed up the scalded milk- that one needed to be looked up online to find the exact meaning!! It does not mean boiling!! The second hurdle was the slightly beaten egg yolks- to incorporate the hot mixture into this, one needs to be diligent and place 2tbsp or 3 to get it tempered and pour into the hot mixture! Then it has to be stirred constantly so it thickens and doesn't burn on the bottom! ***now I know why people use instant pudding!!!*** then lastly the taste was okay- sweet. I skipped the meringue and made fresh whipped cream! That made the dessert! Overall I may not make it in the future..but if you have time and don't mind stirring for almost an hour it'll be good for you!

reviews.review_text: Flavor, texture and taste are FIVE stars. However, the way this is written out as a recipe is unfinished. I am a firm believer of not blaming a chef if I screw up their recipe as it would usually be my fault. But when it comes to baking and you have to, for example, cook a custard, a recipe worth its weight in salt tells you the EXACT size of saucepan you need (if it's too big, your sugar will stick to the bottom and burn no matter how much you stir it, or the ingredients will evaporate) , some sort of guideline as to HOW thick the mixture should be (coats the spoon, leaves a space at the bottom of the pan when you swirl the spoon, etc), approximation of how many minutes the mixture takes to thicken, and this recipe had none of that. I threw out my first mixture and just started over. I used what I figured to be the right size pans (my spaghetti pot for the mixture was WAY too big) kept stirring and just hoped. And I got lucky. It thickened, I put plastic on it (thanks to another reviewer, not the recipe) and it chilled overnight and totally, totally solidified perfectly. It's delicious, looks adorable and homey, and tastes great with whipped cream I made. Great taste, irresponsible recipe.

reviews.review_text:
Made 1 yesterday. HUGE mistake... should have made 2!! We all devoured it and wanted seconds, but none to be had. Followed recipe exactly, except added a tad more flour to make sure it thickened properly, which it indeed did. When I added the beaten egg yolks (after mixing in a bit of the hot mixture) to the entire hot mixture, there seemed to be flecks of yellow in the "batter". Was concerned about this, but once it was refrigerated, they disappeared. Just like the entire pie, within minutes! Yum, yum. I am now in the process of making another one- just waiting for the pie crust (store bought) to cool. I top it with heavy whipping cream beaten with a bit of 10x sugar. Important to get the bowl and beaters chilled before beating your whipping cream. I am impatient, so throw them in the freezer for 5 minutes. Works perfectly every time! This banana cream pie recipe is superb. Reminds me of the banana creme pie of a famous local restaurant, Lucille and Otley's. Unfortunately it is gone, but so glad to be able to make a pie that's equal to theirs. Thanks so much!
(Also, this pie is quite easy to make. The thickening process doesn't take a long time, but do be diligent about stirring.)

Heed my warnings!! If you follow this recipe exactly to the letter, it will not work for you! You will end up like I did with a soupy filling that's not even pudding-like consistency. It tastes good, sure, but did I ask for banana cream soup? No! I wanted pie! My recommendations are to reduce the milk by half a cup and increase the flour by adding a tablespoon at a time, whisking quickly while it's on the stove. Cook the milk/egg/flour/sugar mixture until it reaches honey-like consistency. Don't be afraid to cook beyond 5 mins if you don't think it's thick enough yet. You could even add a couple tablespoons of cornstarch in the beginning (mix cornstarch and a little bit of chilled milk in a cup, then pour into the hot mixture so you don't get clumps). My final tip is to strain the mixture through a fine mesh sieve when it's done cooking, this will catch any stubborn lumps of flour.

The pudding was amazing! I made one and a half batches since I was using a 10" pie dish. I'm glad I did! It filled the dish to the brim, and there were two servings of plain pudding I covered in small glasses for my anti-banana child; I put some whipped cream on it, and he LOVED it! The pie was great! My husband got to the end of his piece and said, "That's going into the dessert repertoire, right?" I would recommend finding some perfectly yellow ripe bananas. My grocery did not have any without some green, so the bananas weren't quite as flavorful as I'd have liked, but that has nothing to do with the recipe. The only thing I changed was the portion of the directions that calls for heating the milk before adding it to the other ingredients. Instead, I did like many other recipes and whisked the dry ingredients with the milk and whipped yolks BEFORE ever turning on the heat. It turns out smooth and eliminates the extra step/time and dirty dishes!

That's going into the dessert repertoire, right?

reviews.review_text:
This recipe is truly delicious. Don't listen to the other reviewers who said this recipe is soupy. They didn't cook the pudding enough. I followed the recipe exactly, but after I incorporated the egg yolks into the custard mixture, I cooked it for another 5-10 minutes over low-med heat. It's ready when the pudding coats the back of the spoon and you can run your finger through it and the line stays put. No drips. Use good vanilla extract for max flavor. I used a vanilla bean.

I added another layer of banana on top of the cooled pie, right before I added a layer of fresh whipped cream and then I chilled the pie for another hour before serving. Added shaved chocolate sprinkles on top for pretty decoration. A HUGE hit!

reviews.review_text: This recipe came out amazing! I followed each step as it it listed and it came out perfect. In fact...this was my very first home-made pie! So much fun. For those who got a "runny" consistency, it just needed to cook longer. I have a gas stove and I had my mixture heating on 3.5 (on a 1-6 scale this was my "medium") and I cooked that for a solid 6 minutes before putting the lid on and cooking the additional 2 minutes. I used a whisk and it was easy to see once it started getting pretty thick. Also, maybe some people poured their mixture in the pie crust before letting it completely cool to room temperature. Once I poured mine in I cooled it in the fridge for about an hour. Whipped cream is always an option but I enjoyed it just as it was:) I will definitely bake again. Thanks Lennie!
